We raised £26,000 for charity through an app where every like was worth 1p. We made exactly £0 in revenue. I was 18. First year of my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs. I met the co-founder in the basement prayer room. We'd just finished praying and I asked him how he was doing, just being polite, and he mistook it as me asking how the app was doing. This man was probably mid-thirties, been at Goldman for years, and he just started telling me about this social media platform where every like triggered a micro-donation to charity. I had no idea what he was talking about. But I was in. That's how MiniDeed started for me. 1p, 2p, 5p. Tiny amounts that added up across 25 countries over two years. We onboarded Islamic Relief, Human Relief Foundation, a bunch of smaller orgs. We got featured in The New Arab. And somehow built a community where people were opening up about mental health because the whole vibe was just different. Users told us it was the only app where they felt safe doing that. Honestly watching the live donation ticker go up was more addictive than any MRR dashboard I've looked at since (and I say that as someone who now stares at dashboards for a living). We never figured out how to make money from it. Donations still trickle through the app daily, years later. But it was my first real taste of building something and I think about it all the time. 18 years old, sitting in Goldman Sachs by day, shipping a charity app by night. It led me to build the highest-rated burger joint in London. And now Draper.

Content is product. Product is content. I've said it maybe 200 times now. Most founders nod and then go do the opposite anyway. We ran Simply Smashed with zero paid marketing. Literally zero. We were just documenting the messiness of building a burger joint from the back of a flower shop and posting it, and that was doing the job a £5k/month ad budget would've done. We became the highest-rated burger spot in London and never boosted a single post. Then MiniDeed happened. The product was good and the impact was real and nobody knew it existed. The thing about having no distribution is it doesn't matter how good your product is. Nobody sees it. Completely opposite outcomes that somehow taught me the exact same thing. The founders who get this are building content into the product from day one. The GTM isn't a department you bolt on in month six, it's the whole thing. If you just raised and you're trying to decide whether to invest in content or put it off, the thing you're actually deferring is distribution.

The best thing I did at Goldman Sachs was talk my way onto someone else's janky side project. Mehti prayed next to me every day. One afternoon on the way out I asked how it was going. I meant it as a greeting. He heard it as a question about his startup, and started telling me everything. He'd coded it himself and it barely worked. The idea was that every like turns into a penny for charity, so content creators could fundraise just by posting. I couldn't stop thinking about it. So I asked if I could work on it. I was 19. The whole company was two co-founders, one engineer, and me. We got into an accelerator called Fast Forward in Stratford. My Goldman apprenticeship was three days work, two days uni, so I started skipping the uni days and going to the programme instead. I didn't have a growth strategy. I just started posting about what we were building on Twitter because it felt like the obvious thing to do. Then I found a hook that made people finally get what MiniDeed was, and one tweet went viral. That turned into a funnel into a Telegram community, and it kept growing on its own. Then Ramadan hit. High profile Muslim creators started reaching out, New Arab, Islam Channel. We ran a campaign and the numbers got kind of mad. 26,000 donations, 800,000 taps, 47,000 posts across 26 countries. oh btw - he never did tell me how he was doing.

food industry is a lot like the bear I had a great chat with Areeb Siddiqui who treated me to a surprise mukbang and went through my journey of building Simply Smashed Smashed we talked about what we’re trying to achieve which is more than flipping burgers check it out👇🏾

I didn’t plan to build Simply Smashed – we built it to survive. In early 2020, just as the lockdown was being announced, my parents boarded a flight back to Bangladesh, leaving my brother, Sifat Ahmed, and me to manage our family’s Italian restaurant in East London. What was meant to be a routine trip turned into a months-long ordeal. Suddenly, we were on our own, struggling to keep the business afloat without knowing when our parents could return. Those months were some of the most intense and challenging of my life. Between finishing my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs, navigating repatriation flights to bring my parents, and even dealing with a burglary at the restaurant, it felt like we were up against a storm. We knew we had to go back to basics. We transformed the delivery experience, launched two critical campaigns, and even got featured on Islam Channel for our efforts to donate pizzas to NHS staff during the pandemic – all while operating from the red. This is why community is one of the foundations of our brand. Simply Smashed was born out of sheer necessity. It wasn’t a start from scratch; it was a start from survival. Today, we're proud to be a family-run business as the highest rated burger joint in London (4.9* 1800+ Google reviews) with a story grounded in resilience and community. Loved speaking to Areeb Siddiqui on his podcast about our journey and what's to come next!

Ever had 20 litres of white sauce spill all over your car? It happened to me. My mum had made a fresh batch of our signature white sauce—my brother Sifat Ahmed’s recipe inspired by his travels to New York and the halal carts there. I was transporting it to the restaurant when we realised the container wasn’t sealed properly. The sauce spilled everywhere. Twenty litres, gone. It felt like a disaster, but we couldn’t salvage the sauce—so we salvaged the situation. Right there, amidst the chaos, we started shooting content. We recorded the mess, the frustration, the absurdity of it all—and then we shared it. That content went viral. Hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok and Instagram. What started as a disaster turned into one of our most successful marketing moments. But the story doesn’t end there. One of my staff recommended his friend’s detailing business to clean up the car, and these boys did such an incredible job that I ended up hiring two of them for front-of-house at Simply Smashed. One of them, just last month, brought in over 100 five-star reviews by himself. When life gives you lemons, make marketing content. Setbacks have a way of leading to unexpected wins. Like the time we raised over £4,000 for charity after getting review-bombed—but that’s a story for another post. What setbacks have you turned into opportunities? Share your story—I’d love to hear it.

Three years ago, we borrowed a projector. This summer, we packed out a living room. When we opened Simply Smashed three years ago, it was during the Euros final. At the time, we were a dark kitchen, but we started getting requests to show the game. So, I borrowed a projector from a friend, put together some tables, and screened the final in-store. It felt like something was missing—a Muslim-friendly atmosphere to watch live sports. That night planted a seed. We weathered the storm as a dark kitchen, built our reputation, and became a Top Eats vendor on Uber Eats, a certification awarded to the platform's highest-performing restaurants. When we finally had enough together, we renovated the space with one clear goal: to create a communal living room. A Muslim-friendly "third space" where people could gather, relax, and feel at home. Fast forward to this summer, and we hosted our second Euros final. Alhamdulillah, we’ve come a long way. We’ve added two screens, brought in sofas, and designed the space ourselves to look and feel like a living room. The atmosphere was incredible, and the place was full. Our vision is to create a true third space for Muslims. If non-Muslims have pubs to see their regular community, why shouldn’t Muslims have something similar? An alcohol-free, music-free space where everyone, Muslim or not, can find their community outside the pub. It’s humbling to reflect on how far we’ve come, and it’s exciting to think about what’s next. Who knows where we’ll be by the next Euros, inshaAllah?

We ban men from eating at our restaurant. Well, on Sisters’ Nights, at least. At Simply Smashed, our Sisters’ Nights are one-of-a-kind: exclusive evenings where only women are allowed to eat in-store. These nights are about more than just food. They create a safe, welcoming space for women to relax, connect, and enjoy themselves. Our most recent Sisters’ Night was a collaboration with Shabbir Hassan’s Faith Space, where we hosted a Palestinian-themed evening. Faith Space brought in Palestinian speakers to share their stories, and 50% of the night’s proceeds were donated to Human Aid & Advocacy’s Gaza Appeal. Initiatives like these tie directly into the larger mission of Simply Smashed: elevating the standards of Muslim entrepreneurship. Why do we do things like Sisters’ Nights? Because the best way to inspire change isn’t by telling others what to do—it’s by leading with action. Since launching Sisters’ Nights, we’ve already seen other restaurants follow the trend and host their own versions. And that’s the goal. To show that initiatives like these are not only meaningful but commercially viable. And if they’re commercially viable, you’ll see other businesses follow—something we know all too well in the Muslim food industry. This is part of our wider approach of building with barakah and injecting creativity to inspire others. It’s about setting trends that strengthen our communities and create lasting change. If you’ve been to one of our Sisters’ Nights, we’d love to hear your thoughts. And if not—keep an eye out for the next one. PS: What do you think of the banner? Can anyone guess which brand I got inspiration from for the copy? (Hint: It’s from a chocolate.)

If you’ve got bad breath, we’ll give you a discount. Okay, not quite—but if you’re fasting on Mondays and Thursdays, you can claim 30% off during Maghrib time as part of our Winter Arc Campaign, which launched today at Simply Smashed. The idea behind this campaign actually started when I was 20. Back then, I ran a small campaign to encourage winter fasting. I designed a simple poster with a friend, left it in Islamic society prayer rooms alongside boxes of dates, and shared it online. Before I knew it, others were replicating it in their own spaces. That experience taught me something profound: small, intentional acts can inspire meaningful change. Fast forward six years, and we’re building on that same idea—this time through Simply Smashed. The Winter Arc Campaign isn’t just about discounts. It’s about encouraging good. It’s about making fasting feel accessible and inspiring, especially for younger Muslims. The early response has been incredible. Within hours, the campaign hit 1.2k likes on TikTok. People are sharing how Simply Smashed encourages them to reconnect with their values. To make it even more impactful, we partnered with the imam of East London Mosque & London Muslim Centre who shared a heartfelt reminder on the virtues of fasting. At Simply Smashed, we rarely offer discounts. When we do, it’s always tied to a clear purpose. Campaigns like this reflect our mission: to build with barakah, inspire others, and serve our communities in ways that align with our faith. If this campaign inspires even one person to fast, that’s a success. If it inspires others to create similar initiatives in their own spaces, that’s barakah. Let’s encourage more barakah based building.

Last night, we went from London’s highest-rated to possibly the UK’s highest-rated burger joint. 6 months ago, we became London’s highest-rated burger joint, sitting at 4.8⭐️ with 1,000 reviews. But milestones aren’t where you stop. They’re where you push harder. As of last night, we’ve reached 4.9⭐️ with 2,000 reviews—a milestone that reflects so much more than just numbers. This is about a vision my team and I hold dearly: to uplift standards, to inspire ourselves and others, and to show what happens when you strive for ihsan (excellence) every single day. We’ve always believed that the best time to double down is when you’re already winning. That’s the heart of barakah-based building—creating with intention, delivering with excellence, and ensuring every step we take is meaningful and impactful. I’m deeply grateful for everyone who’s been part of this journey. Every review, every kind word, and every bit of love you’ve shown has helped us reach this point. You’ve made it clear that Simply Smashed is more than just a burger joint—it’s a space built on community, values, and striving to be the best. Oh, and about that sticker on our window proudly proclaiming “Number 1 in London with 1,000+ reviews”? Maybe it’s time we update it. After all, going from number 1 to staying number 1 is worth celebrating. And we’re just getting started, inshaAllah. Let’s keep raising the bar together.

For many young Muslims, the Christmas season can feel isolating. The celebrations around them can make it seem like there’s nothing for them to take part in—like their Muslim identity holds them back. I want to change that. At Simply Smashed we’ve always said that whatever happens outside our doors—whether people feel uncomfortable, insecure, or confused about their Muslim identity—inside Simply Smashed, that identity isn’t just tolerated. It’s celebrated. That’s the heart of our Fajr Nights campaign. Here’s how it works: During the holiday period, kids who attend 10 consecutive Fajr prayers at their local masjid and get their attendance cards stamped by their imam will earn a free meal at Simply Smashed. It’s about more than the meal. It’s about helping kids build the habit of Fajr, yes—but it’s also about giving them a sense of pride and belonging. We want young Muslims to know that our tradition has its own beauty, that our community is something to celebrate, and that there is something for them during this season. The masjid is where they’ll feel that sense of community. And Simply Smashed is where we’ll reward and celebrate their efforts. Being Muslim doesn’t mean missing out. It means embracing something even greater. What are your thoughts on creating spaces that celebrate identity and community?

We turned our burger joint into a classroom for young French Muslims. For the second year running, Simply Smashed has hosted French exchange students, with my brother, Sifat Ahmed, teaching them English during the day while they explore London in the evenings. But this is about more than just learning a language. Growing up in Dieppe, a small seaside town in France, we didn’t have many Muslims around us. Finding community was tough, and balancing our French and Muslim identities was even harder. Sifat has been volunteering with this French exchange group Oui Love Trips for years because we know how valuable it is to have spaces where you feel comfortable as a young Muslim. Simply Smashed has become that space. A place where these kids can not only learn but feel proud of who they are. It feels like coming full circle. This is what the communal living room was designed for. To create a space where being Muslim feels normal. Where young Muslims can feel seen, heard, and celebrated.

The scrolls are here. The Quest for Fajr Knights begins. A scroll delivered to young warriors, calling them to rise with the dawn. This isn’t just about a free meal. It’s about creating a legacy, shaping habits, and showing the next generation that their faith is something to celebrate. Here’s the mission: • Pray Fajr every day for 10 days during the holidays. • Get your attendance card stamped by your local Imam. • Complete the quest and earn your reward—a feast fit for champions. Last year, Fajr Knights was simply an idea. This year, it’s a movement. We’ve added scrolls to turn the challenge into an adventure, making kids feel like heroes on a quest—because that’s exactly what they are. For too long, young Muslims have felt like bystanders during the festive season. Fajr Knights reminds them that our traditions are worth celebrating. It brings them back to the masjid, to their community, and shows them that staying connected to faith is its own reward. This isn’t just what Simply Smashed does—it’s who we are. We’re here to build more than just burger joints. We’re here to build pride, joy, and community. The scrolls have found their knights. Will they rise to the challenge? The journey begins at Fajr.

This weekend, I’ve been building something I’ve dreamed about for years. Young Muslims face so much emotionally, especially during their teenage years. Some of us were lucky to have an "Ameen" in our lives. That person in the prayer room who gave the right advice at the right time. But many didn’t have that privilege. So I built Ameen, your Muslim companion. Ameen provides comfort, shares relevant duas, and offers lessons from the Seerah. It’s not about fatwas or rulings—it’s about support when it’s needed most. I spent the weekend rapidly prototyping and shipped an MVP (check comments). It’s simple, not perfect, but that’s the point. The goal is to iterate quickly, collect feedback, and build something that genuinely resonates with its users. This same product thinking is what built Simply Smashed into the UK’s highest-rated burger joint. From data-driven menu designs to understanding what our community values most, product thinking has always been central to what I do. Even though Simply Smashed keeps me busy, I’ve missed building products like this. It’s about identifying a problem, understanding the user, and delivering value fast. Also, I’ve also been expanding my design skills as a product manager. Ameen has been a great way to put that into practice and push myself creatively while solving meaningful problems. Accuracy will get better but check it out now in the comments, what do you think?

A child stood up and led a talk after Fajr this morning. At Darul Arqam, our partner mosque, the Fajr Knights programme is in full swing. Kids are waking up for Fajr, sharing naseeha (advice) with each other, and strengthening their bond as a community. One child even led a talk today—a moment that reflected the confidence and leadership we hope to nurture. Afterwards, they shared breakfast provided by the mosque, laughing and enjoying the sense of connection these mornings are creating. When I was younger, trips to restaurants were special because they were such rare occasions. It’s those types of memories that stick with you—moments of joy, community, and pride. That’s what we hope to create and leave behind for these kids. This is what Fajr Knights is all about—not just prayer, but fostering community, identity, and pride. Looking forward to hosting the winners at Simply Smashed soon. But honestly? The real victory is seeing what’s happening right now.

The hidden cost of Muslim businesses chasing "white validation"... A disturbing pattern I've noticed in London's Muslim-owned restaurants: I recently spoke to a Muslim café owner who said "too many Muslims moving into the area is ruining business." Another Muslim Italian spot owner proudly poured wine while telling me "we only have high quality customers here." This isn't just about serving alcohol. It's about a colonial mindset that's still living rent-free in our community's heads. Success gets measured by how many white customers come through the door. Values get compromised for validation. Look at Brick Lane: • Muslim-owned restaurants all serving alcohol • Most struggling to stay afloat • None questioning why their barakah feels empty They change their names for acceptance. They change their values for profit. They change their whole identity for a pat on the back. Part of me understands - many did this to survive in a different era. But the real damage? Their children are watching. They're learning that success means shrinking yourself. Growing up thinking you need to be less Muslim to be more successful. That's exactly why I built Simply Smashed differently. I wanted to prove you can run a proper food spot, stay true to your values, and still win. No alcohol. No compromise. Just great food and real community. The result? We get everyone through our doors - Muslims, non-Muslims, families, young professionals. Why? Because when you're confident in who you are, people respect that. We don't need validation from serving wine. We get it from serving great food and staying true to our principles. The next generation needs to see this. Success doesn't mean becoming less of who you are. It means being exactly who Allah made you to be. If you're building a halal business, remember: Your principles are your competitive advantage, not your limitation.

The most dangerous thing you can do is put successful people on a pedestal. Here's why pedestals kill dreams, and what to do instead: I used to think successful people were built different. That they had some special DNA that made them capable of achieving incredible things. But after building multiple businesses, I've realized something profound: Pedestals create mental barriers that stop you from achieving your dreams. When you put someone on a pedestal, you subconsciously tell yourself their success is unreachable. You create an imaginary gap between you and them that doesn't exist. The truth? They're just regular people who: • Failed countless times • Learned from mistakes • Stayed consistent • Picked the right moments Here's another dangerous thing about pedestals: When we put people on them, they start believing they have all the answers. Just because someone built a successful tech company doesn't mean they know the secret to happiness. Just because someone's great at marketing doesn't mean they understand the meaning of life. Success in one area doesn't equal wisdom in all areas. The moment I stopped putting successful people on pedestals, everything changed. Their achievements suddenly felt within reach. My ambitions started feeling achievable. Instead of seeing them as distant role models, I started seeing them as future peers. And here's the crazy part - when you shift this mindset, they naturally become your peers. So here's what you should do instead: Turn those pedestals into ladders. Break down exactly what made them successful: • Study their specific traits • Analyze their decisions • Learn from their mistakes • Copy their winning moves Because here's the truth: Everyone is human. Everyone has flaws. And everything they've achieved is within your reach. The question is: Are you going to sit back and admire from a distance? Or are you ready to start climbing? ↓ If this resonated, follow me for more insights on building businesses and achieving your dreams. I share everything I learn from running Simply Smashed, London's highest-rated smash burger joint, and other ventures.

I turned down franchise requests from Dubai and Toronto yesterday. Here's why saying no to fast money might be the best business decision you make: I've watched too many Muslim-owned food brands expand rapidly, only to collapse spectacularly. Two years ago, I sat in a franchise pitch meeting that opened my eyes. The presenters were ex-bankers who claimed they'd "cracked" the burger game. 90% of their pitch wasn't about the food or brand - it was about investment protection schemes and rapid expansion plans. That should have been the first red flag. But for many in our community, especially those struggling to adapt to the changing hospitality landscape, it looked impressive. Polished ex-bankers. Protected investments. Rapid growth promises. That brand doesn't exist anymore. And here's the tragic part: The owners walked away with their franchise fees. But the franchisees? They're left picking up the pieces. This pattern keeps repeating: • Quick franchise sales • Minimal support • Failed locations • Lost life savings That's why at Simply Smashed, we're taking a different approach: We won't expand until we're 100% ready. We're not just building a burger brand. We're building a legacy that needs to match the quality of our product. We're focused on optimising everything before we even think about scaling. Sometimes the bravest business decision is saying "not yet" to opportunity. ↓ If you believe in building sustainably over scaling quickly, follow me for more insights on principled business growth.

We gamified Quran memorization with burgers and milkshakes. Here's why 100+ huffadh are loving it: Walking through East London Mosque, you see them everywhere. Brothers in corners perfecting every ayah of the Quran. Some staying up late, others coming at Fajr. Many of us struggle to just finish reading the Quran during Ramadan. But these huffadh (memorizers) perfect it completely - verse by verse, chapter by chapter. And they do this every single year. Most don't realize the sacrifice: • Months away from family • Time off work • Countless hours of revision • Mental strain of perfection That's why we launched our "Road to Ramadan" campaign at Simply Smashed. We've gamified their Quran revision journey: • 5 chapters = Punch on our machine • 10 chapters = Milkshake • 15 chapters = Tiramisu • 20 chapters = Wings • 25 chapters = Loaded fries • Complete Quran = Everything + burger We're partnering with Europe's largest gathering of huffadh - where hundreds come to revise. When we started Simply Smashed, people said "just focus on the burgers." But it was never just about the food. We're about recognizing the people in our community who don't get enough recognition. The ones who sacrifice silently. The ones who serve others without praise. That's what barakah-based building means to us. Not maximizing profits. Maximizing impact. Sometimes that means Sisters' Nights. Sometimes Fajr Knights. And sometimes it means supporting those who preserve the words of Allah. It might not be much, but it's our way of saying: We see your dedication. We appreciate your sacrifice. ↓ This Ramadan, let's show our huffadh they're valued. Drop by Simply Smashed to support their journey and maybe catch them taking a well-deserved break between revisions.

These teenage brothers just recited the entire Quran from memory in 9 hours - finishing just 2 seconds apart. Here's why their story matters to our entire community: At dawn, Abdurrahman (15) and Saabiq (16) began their extraordinary challenge. Hour after hour, verse after verse, they raced through 6,236 verses purely from memory. By 4:30pm, they had achieved what takes most people years to accomplish. Their father walked through our doors, eyes gleaming with joy, his sons' achievement radiating through his proud smile. We've partnered with Quran Revision Project - Europe's largest gathering of Huffadh - for our Road to Ramadan campaign, offering free meals to these dedicated memorizers of the Quran. But this isn't just about food. It's about recognition. It's about saying: "We see you." Our Huffadh represent something profound in our community: The preservation of our heritage. The bridge between generations. The future of our spiritual leadership. Yet too often, these young champions go unrecognized: • Years of dawn-to-dusk dedication • Sacrificing typical teenage experiences • Balancing intense memorization with school • Carrying the weight of religious responsibility at such a young age This Ramadan, they'll lead Taraweeh prayers at their local mosque in Barking. Think about that - at 15 and 16, they'll guide hundreds in prayer. At Simply Smashed, we believe business isn't just about transactions. It's about strengthening the fabric of our community. It's about creating spaces where achievements like these are celebrated. Where young people feel seen, valued, and supported. Because when we uplift our youth, we elevate our entire community. When we celebrate their dedication, we inspire the next generation. When we show them we're proud, we give them the strength to continue. ↓ This Ramadan, let's commit to appreciating our Huffadh more. They're not just memorizing text - they're preserving our heritage, one verse at a time. Share this to show our young Huffadh: Your community stands with you. We see you. And we are incredibly proud.

Lost 1000 Google reviews in 7 days. Our rating dropped from 4.9 to 4.8. But here's why I stayed calm - we've been here before: Last year, Uber Eats wiped out ALL 4,000 of our reviews without warning. We were the top-rated restaurant. Then suddenly... nothing. But here's what happened next: Within 2 months, we climbed back to top-rated status. Why? Because great businesses aren't built on reviews. They're built on processes. This week's Google review disappearance felt familiar: 2337 → 2000 → 1800 → 1600. No explanation. No warning. Just watching our social proof vanish. But I felt an unusual sense of peace. When you've rebuilt from zero before, you learn what truly matters: • Reviews don't build great businesses - processes do • External validation is temporary - excellence is permanent • Numbers can disappear - quality never does At Simply Smashed, we've built a culture of ihsan (excellence). This means: • Never resting on our laurels • Constantly improving our systems • Focusing on what we can control • Building something that lasts The technical glitch resolved itself today. We're back to being the UK's highest-rated burger joint. But the lesson remains: Build your foundation on rock-solid processes, not fleeting metrics. Because when the metrics disappear (and trust me, they sometimes will), your processes will keep you standing. ↓ If you're building something meaningful, follow along for more insights on purpose-driven growth.

I hobbled across a busy London road with 3 stacked burgers, wearing a protective boot. The journey from photoshoot to London's highest-rated burger joint taught me 5 crucial lessons: When we started, we couldn't afford professional photography. So there I was, against doctor's orders, in a protective boot, balancing burgers in traffic. But that's what it takes. Here's what I learned: 1. Start with what you have Don't wait for perfect conditions. We used an iPhone, natural light, and pure determination. Your resourcefulness matters more than your resources. 2. Pain is temporary, regret is forever My foot needed rest, but my dream needed action. Sometimes you have to push through temporary discomfort for long-term success. 3. Documentation is crucial Those early photos? They became our first marketing materials. Every struggle is content. Every setback is a story. Document your journey. 4. Consistency compounds We showed up every single day. Even when sales were low. Even when we were exhausted. Even when it felt pointless. The result? We became London's highest-rated burger joint in just 12 months. 5. Your 'why' must be bigger than your excuses We weren't just building a restaurant. We were creating a space where quality meets community, where halal food meets innovation. The most important lesson? There are no days off when you're building something you're truly passionate about. But passion alone isn't enough - it's the daily grind, the unsexy work, the showing up when nobody's watching that makes the difference. ↓ If you're in London and want to taste what happens when passion meets persistence, visit us at Simply Smashed.

We got review bombed for supporting Palestine, so we doubled down - now we're UK's #1 rated burger joint. I remember when we first started getting review-bombed. One-star reviews started trickling in. No comments, just stars. Then we saw the pattern: People targeting us because we chose to stock Salam Cola (which donates 10% to Palestine) over mainstream alternatives. Their message was clear: "The food industry shouldn't be involved in politics." But here's what they didn't understand: When your entire supply chain shares your values (from butchers to distributors), and your customer base shares your values, the only thing silencing you is yourself. So we decided to flip the script. Within 4 days, we: • Launched a special burger campaign • Partnered with Muslim Aid UK • Donated 100% of profits to Gaza • Doubled down on our partnership with Salaam Cola France The result? Over £4,000 raised in just one week. But more importantly, our community rallied behind us with thousands of genuine 5-star reviews. This taught me something profound about business: Many Muslim business owners operate from fear: • Fear of standing out • Fear of rocking the boat • Fear of losing customers But here's the truth: If your values align with your community, standing firm only makes you stronger. That's why Simply Smashed isn't just a burger joint. We're setting a new standard for Muslim businesses: • Prayer rooms in our restaurant • Sisters-only dining nights • Quran recitation in our content • Unapologetic support for causes we believe in The best part? Other restaurants are following suit. Because the best way to change an industry isn't through force. It's by showing there's a better way. ↓ If you enjoyed this, follow me for more insights on building value-driven businesses.

Why we're closing our restaurant for the first week of Ramadan... And why it'll cost us 30% of our monthly revenue: Most restaurants are rushing to capitalize on Iftar sales right now. We're doing the opposite. At Simply Smashed, we've made it a tradition to close during Ramadan's first week. Here's why: Iftar service is brutal. Imagine 50+ concurrent orders hitting simultaneously, all made fresh to order. Our team works incredibly hard during this month, managing both their fasts and intense service periods. So we give them this time to: • Reset mentally • Connect with family • Focus on their spiritual journey But we don't stop there. Throughout Ramadan, we only open an hour before Iftar. No daytime operations. No pressure on our fasting staff. These decisions cost us about 20-30% of our usual monthly revenue. But you know what? Values > Profits. I've worked through many Ramadans before starting this business. I know how challenging it can be to balance work and worship during this sacred month. That's why, as we've grown, we've intentionally built these accommodations into our business model. It might not be what maximizes profit. But it maximizes barakah (blessing). And that's the foundation we're building on. ↓ If you're interested in learning more about how we're building a values-first business, follow me for regular insights on ethical entrepreneurship.

The UK has a prayer space problem—and we've all felt it. Many restaurants market iftar deals for Ramadan, but forget the most important part—a place to pray. Picture this: You're out for iftar. The restaurant's packed with Muslims breaking their fast. Maghrib time comes... but there's nowhere to pray. And it's not just Ramadan. Mosques closed between jama'ah. Tight salah windows in winter. Sisters left with even fewer options. We can do better. We must do better. That's why at Simply Smashed, prayer spaces have been available since we first opened our doors. Last month, we made it our pledge that every future Simply Smashed location will have a dedicated place to pray. Every Simply Smashed location offers a place to pray—brothers and sisters alike. Just ask our staff, and we'll make it happen. And here's the key part: You don't have to be a customer. If you need to pray, our doors are open for you. We know mosques are doing their best. Many are donation-based and rely on volunteers, making it difficult to stay open all day. That's where businesses like ours can step in to help fill the gaps. This is about more than burgers. We're committed to making prayer spaces available everywhere we grow: • Every Simply Smashed location has dedicated prayer facilities, alhamdulillah • We ensure both brothers and sisters have equal, dignified spaces • Our staff are trained to help facilitate prayer space access • Prayer mats are always available and clean No Muslim should have to miss salah or pray in a car park because they couldn't find a space. No sister should feel anxious about where she'll pray Asr during a shopping trip. No one should have to choose between breaking their fast at a restaurant and making maghrib prayer on time. This is our open prayer policy. But our vision goes beyond us. Imagine a network of accessible prayer spaces across the UK—cafés, restaurants, and businesses creating solutions for the community. This is our step forward, and we hope it inspires others to join us. We build with barakah, and we're proud to serve our community in more ways than one. Check us out at Simply Smashed and follow along as we continue building with barakah 🙏🏾

We're revolutionising the iftar experience at UK's highest-rated burger joint. Here's what I've been building during our break, ready for our reopening this Friday (March 7th): Most restaurants just feed your body during Ramadan. We're feeding your soul too. I've spent these off-days crafting something unique: a digital countdown clock that transforms the iftar experience: Instead of just showing time until sunset, it displays carefully curated spiritual reminders: • Words that touch the heart • Reflections that prepare the soul • Gentle prompts to maximise these blessed moments All while ambient vocal-only beats create a peaceful atmosphere throughout the restaurant. Imagine walking into Simply Smashed as sunset approaches: • Soft traditional lights dance across the walls • Incense perfumes drift through the space • Spiritual reminders illuminate the space • Families and friends gather around tables, nourishing body and soul We've engineered every detail of your iftar experience: Complimentary mouthwash shots for everyone heading to taraweeh prayer. Prayer facilities always open, welcoming anyone who needs a quiet moment. This approach comes from a simple truth: At London's highest-rated burger joint, we don't just serve food. We create moments that matter. Where faith meets innovation. Where every detail enhances your worship. Where Ramadan joy is visible, tangible, and contagious. ↓ Join us this Friday as we reopen with this enhanced Ramadan experience. Tag someone who needs to know about this.

I built an ugly restaurant that became UK's highest-rated burger joint. Here's why that was intentional: When you walk past Simply Smashed, you'll see a temporary banner with some red paint. Inside? A buzzing atmosphere and the best burgers in town. This wasn't an accident - it was strategy. Most restaurants do it backwards: Beautiful exterior first, then figure out the food. We focused on perfecting our product before touching the aesthetics. Every penny went into iterating our recipes, improving our systems, and delighting our customers. We were transparent with everyone: "This isn't our final form." The result? • Highest-rated burger joint in UK • Cult-like following • Customers who trust our journey The exterior will match the interior soon. But only after we've achieved the perfect product. Too many businesses focus on looking good before being good. They burn through customers who judge the book by its cover, then never return. We chose the opposite path: • Build trust first • Perfect the product • Then make it pretty The lesson? Substance over style, always. Your business might not look perfect yet. But if you're relentlessly improving what matters most, the aesthetics can wait. ↓ Follow me for more insights on building businesses with purpose. Excited to share what's next for Simply Smashed.

Yes. I am the face of that meme you see every Ramadan... The story of how my face became a global Muslim internet phenomenon: I'm that guy from the "When you're fasting but..." meme. You know, the one that resurfaces every single Ramadan across multiple countries. One of the wildest moments? Standing in line for Fajr prayer and seeing someone scrolling through that meme on their phone. Right next to me. The story behind it is pretty simple: I made a joke post when I was 15. Not even based on real experience - just something my friend and I thought would be funny. But it took on a life of its own. The meme has been translated into languages I can't even read. It's been remixed into marriage posts (because Muslim Twitter always finds a way). People have twisted it, turned it, and transformed it into their own versions. Every Ramadan, without fail, it comes back in new forms. Screenshots, reposts, tags - crossing cultural and language barriers I never imagined. At first, I wasn't sure how to feel about being an international meme. Then I had a realization: If life gives you viral memes, use them. So we recreated the entire meme inside Simply Smashed, our restaurant. Complete with my dad in the shot (yes, he's a good sport). Sometimes your biggest "embarrassments" can become opportunities. You just have to lean into them. ↓ If you enjoyed this story, follow me for more insights on building a brand that stands out (even if it starts with becoming a global meme phenomenon).

How we built London's highest-rated burger joint with 8,500+ five-star reviews using product development principles instead of culinary training. Our secret? Obsession with data-driven iteration. From my product management background, I applied rapid testing methodology to burger creation. Our first burgers were terrible. We started by giving them to friends and family with one instruction: "Don't hold back." After incorporating their feedback, we moved to real customers, sharing our journey openly on social media. Six months in, with costs mounting and improvements seeming marginal, we almost abandoned the approach. But we persisted, collecting data on every aspect of the burger experience for 18 months straight. We didn't guess what customers wanted - we measured it. What seemed like small details made massive differences: • Testing different bun-to-patty thickness ratios for the perfect bite • Discovering that two pickles created better balance than three • Finding the perfect sauce-to-patty ratio through dozens of variations Our data revealed something surprising: customers preferred fewer, more perfected options. So we eliminated customization and whittled down from dozens of combinations to just three signature burgers. Each of these three burgers represents hundreds of iterations, refined by thousands of data points. The reviews started pouring in: • 2,500+ Google reviews • 6,000+ Uber Eats reviews • Highest-rated burger joint status in London (possibly UK) When our Uber Eats reviews were completely wiped due to a platform issue, I wasn't worried. Within just three months, we regained "Top Eats" status - their highest merchant rating. That's when I knew our system worked perfectly. What makes our approach different: • Family-owned with family-developed recipes • Product development mindset applied to food • Every decision backed by customer data • Systems that could rebuild reputation quickly when needed This approach didn't just create better burgers - it built a resilient business. Our customer loyalty grew with each iteration as we earned their trust through consistent quality. Now, I'm looking to expand our delivery radius across London and eventually the UK. I'm seeking commercial partners with established delivery networks who are equally ambitious and can match our vision for the next 2-3 years. We have the systems in place now - we need partners who can support our growth while maintaining our obsessive quality standards. If you're a delivery platform interested in bringing London's highest-rated burgers to more customers, let's connect. The lesson extends beyond food: When you obsessively iterate based on real customer data and build systems that can withstand challenges, you create products people can't stop talking about.

My mum spent months obsessing over YouTube tiramisu videos. Testing recipes. Adjusting ratios. Hand-soaking ladyfingers until she got it perfect. My brother had spotted something every Italian restaurant in London missed: every tiramisu contained alcohol, leaving the Muslim community with no options. So he got my mum obsessing in our home kitchen 12 years ago, before Simply Smashed even existed. Her perfectionism created London's first halal tiramisu. Then COVID hit our Italian restaurant. Dining died overnight. Revenue vanished. Staff went home. But we had something special: a 12-year-old innovation that filled a gap others ignored. We launched tiramisu delivery across London - full trays of 24 slices for families and celebrations. The "tiramisu response unit" drove 40% of our revenue during the hardest months. That pivot saved us. After COVID, we opened Simply Smashed, and this dessert became our signature - the perfect finish after a hearty meal. The traits I inherited from my family: • My mom's obsession with perfection (months of testing until it's exactly right) • My brother's ability to spot cultural market gaps (seeing what others miss) • The belief that real innovation starts in the home kitchen, not a boardroom That same process is happening right now. A couple days ago for Eid, my mom was back in the same home kitchen, months into perfecting our new pistachio tiramisu. Testing different pistachio ratios, adjusting the cream texture, making sure every layer brings that same joy our original recipe has delivered for over a decade. She's treating this new flavor with the same obsessive care that saved our business during COVID. The same kitchen. The same perfectionism. The same family innovation process that created London's first halal tiramisu. This week, we're finally ready to share that joy with everyone else. We're launching pistachio tiramisu at Simply Smashed - another family creation moving from our home to your table. Sometimes the smallest innovations create the biggest moments of joy. So excited to share a slice of our Eid joy back to our customers, would love to hear your feedback!

Charity has become too easy. And that's the problem. We've turned giving into a finger tap, losing what it means to help. Here's why we need to bring back physical giving: Everything's been abstracted away. Tap to donate. Swipe to give. Click to help. This convenience comes at a cost that goes deeper than we realize. Research suggests that physical acts of giving may activate different reward pathways in our brains compared to digital donations. When we physically hand over our contribution, we get psychological feedback that a simple tap can't replicate. But it's not just individual psychology. Physical giving rebuilds social fabric. This aligns with what we believe at Simply Smashed - that giving rebuilds community. That's why we're partnering with HumanAid on this Syria relief campaign. Instead of digital donations, we set up a physical drop-off point where people bring food, toiletries, clothes, and nappies. I started this just a couple days ago and the container is already nearly full. The community has really showed up. I've watched a ripple effect happen in real-time. One person brings donations, their neighbor sees them loading the car and stops to ask about it. The psychological shift is visible. People arrive planning to drop off one bag, then see the community response and return later with more. Digital giving requires one decision. Physical giving requires dozens - what to bring, when to go, how much to carry. Commitment psychology research shows that each choice deepens investment in the outcome. This doesn't mean digital giving is worthless. For people with disabilities, busy schedules, or limited resources, online donations are often the only viable option. But for those who can choose, there's something irreplaceable about showing up. These containers go directly to those in need, but the real value is bringing people together around shared purpose. We have until 27th June as a drop-off point, so just 3 more days left. If you're in the area and want to contribute, there's still time. Physical giving creates stories. Digital giving creates receipts. Next time you want to help, consider showing up instead of just paying up. Find a local drive, volunteer at a food bank, or organize something in your neighborhood. Your presence matters as much as your money.

"You're the Palestinian burger guy, right?" 8 hours of interrogation. That's how I knew we were onto something. Three weeks ago, Ibrahim Javed and I tried to cross into the West Bank. Routine questions became an 8-hour detention. Separated rooms. Aggressive searches. They'd found our Simply Smashed campaigns, Palestine flags, Gaza fundraising, everything we thought was "just charity work from a burger joint." Then the interrogator snapped. Started hurling abuse. Told me to "get the f*** out of his country." Here's the thing: He cracked. I didn't. Ibrahim and I walked out and burst into laughter. Not from humour but from validation. They'd just proven our "small" actions had real impact. When charity drives from a burger joint trigger 8-hour government detention? Your "small" actions aren't small at all. Every campaign compounds. Every stand creates ripples they can't ignore. But here's what happened next: Still processing our rejection, Ibrahim and I immediately started talking solutions. Technical platforms for community organizing. Tools to counter systemic discrimination. Solutions to address what we'd just experienced firsthand. The same system that spent 8 hours trying to discourage us accidentally energized us to build even more. Two builders, detained for what they called "small" activism, walking away planning solutions that weren't small at all. That's when it hit me: We spend years perfecting our craft. Chasing ARR. Building unicorns for investors. But our communities don't need more donated profit margins. They need builders using their skills where it matters most. The same product thinking that scales startups? It can scale justice. That's why I'm proud to support the team running Deen Developers's Hack for Gaza. Because the best validation isn't an 8-hour interrogation. It's building solutions so powerful they make interrogations irrelevant. Your skills are your superpower. Time to use them. Join us. Ask any uncle that owns a restaurant: they hate the sunshine. Growing up Bengali, I thought they were just being dramatic. Now I run my own restaurant and I finally get it. Heatwaves kill burger sales. People want milkshakes, not sizzling patties. They want cold drinks, not steaming fries. Last month, I watched my usually busy team waiting around for orders during lunch rush. That's when it hit me like a punch to the gut. This is the quiet anxiety my dad's generation has carried for decades. The seasonal dread they never talk about but always feel. Every sunny weekend, watching revenue drop while rent stays the same. But here's what I learned from watching my dad survive 30 years in this game: The best don't fight the weather. They dance with it. This summer, we completely flipped our approach at Simply Smashed. New blended soft serve shakes made with pure ice cream. Nostalgic flavors like custard and rhubarb that transport you back to childhood summers. New pacha drinks with coconut, mango, and passion fruit. We secured those suppliers first because that's what we do. Our pistachio tiramisu my mum perfected for Eid? Perfect timing for hot weather dessert cravings. And I've been obsessing over something special for 2 months that's about to drop. A grilled chicken creation inspired by my Goldman Sachs office lunch days that I can't wait to share. Milkshake sales jumped 40% in five weeks. The same seasonal "problem" that used to stress me out? It's now driving innovation. My dad taught me something without saying it: survivors don't just endure the seasons - they use them to get stronger. That uncle who hates sunshine? He's stuck fighting the weather. We're using it to prove why we're London's highest-rated burger joint. Sometimes the best business advice comes disguised as family anxiety. The wisdom was always there. I just needed to stop dismissing it as "uncle worries."

There's this lunch from my Goldman days I can't get out of my head. After 16 failed attempts, I finally know why. You know that feeling when you can't get a taste out of your head? That's what happened to me with this lunch I had 5 years ago at Goldman. There was this Peruvian place near our office. Always had these mental queues outside. I'm talking senior bankers, MDs, people who expense £300 dinners without blinking - all standing in line for chicken. One day I thought let me see what all the fuss is about. That green sauce hit me like a truck. I'm not even joking. It was so addictive I understood why grown men in Savile Row suits would abandon their desks for this. The chicken? Fell apart with a fork. Juice running down my wrist. I threw away my Tesco meal deal routine that same day. Fast forward to now. We're London's highest-rated burger joint. But here's the thing - and this is what people don't get about running Simply Smashed - the bar keeps getting higher with every single product we launch. I'm never satisfied. There's this insecurity that drives me mental. This feeling that our products aren't good enough yet. So when I couldn't shake that taste memory, I knew I had to do something about it. What if we took that inspiration and made it our own? Version 1? Complete disaster. Burnt chicken, perfect sauce, everything else wrong. By Version 16, I was losing my mind. Two months of testing marinades. Custom potato buns because our brioche was overpowering the flavors. Different cooking methods to lock in every drop of moisture. Then last week everything clicked. Our green sauce - inspired by Peru but uniquely ours. Same addictive quality but adapted for this burger. When our first customer tried it, he just looked at me wide-eyed and said "This is the best burger on your menu. How did you even make this?" That feeling? When something that's been living in your head becomes real and makes someone else happy? That's why I do this. The Peruvian Thigh launches today. Some obsessions are worth chasing. The best ones change everything when you finally catch them.

The Peruvian Thigh sold out in 3 hours on Monday. Most founders would be celebrating. I'm spending my days restocking and my evenings doing something most people don't realise restaurants need to do. Restocked at 8pm yesterday. Down to 2 left today. I'm literally restocking again as I write this. While everyone's buzzing about the 9s and 10s out of 10 we're getting, I spent yesterday doing the thing I can't stop myself from doing. 4 hours on the floor. Talking to every single customer who ordered it. Not because anything's wrong - the feedback has been insane. People are losing their minds over how tender the chicken is. Sure, one or two people said it wasn't for them. That happens. But here's what nobody tells you about launching food products: The recipe is maybe 20% of the work. The other 80%? Building systems so your staff don't ruin it. This isn't home cooking. You can't just hand someone a recipe and expect magic. I'm spending the next 2 months training every cook on exact timing. Quality control checkpoints. How to handle the marinade. When the chicken is perfectly done vs. overdone. The real skill isn't making good food. It's cutting through the noise of feedback to find what actually matters. Every "this is perfect" gets weighed against every valid criticism. What are people actually saying? What do they mean? How do we take all this data and find the one thing that improves our product? Our first Simply Smashed burger? Complete disaster. Not because the recipe was bad, but because we had no systems. No training. No quality control. I'm not a chef. But I know how to learn. How to gather feedback. How to iterate. It's very easy to get lost in the "yay, we launched a burger" celebration. But that's not it. It's the obsessiveness. The continuous improvement. The gathering data. Making sure we've got the systems in place. It's not sexy work, but it has to be done. While competitors are already planning their next launch, I'm still perfecting Monday's systems. Excellence isn't just a recipe - it's a system that delivers it every single time.

We sold burgers from the back of a flower shop. And it saved our restaurant. Our full-service Italian restaurant was dying after COVID hit. My brother had what seemed like the worst idea ever: "Let's share space with a flower shop and focus on delivery only." I thought he'd lost his mind. Our runway was coming to an end. But when you're drowning, you grab any lifeline. He found the perfect partner - a flower shop that donated profits to Pakistani hospitals. Value-aligned. Rent-splitting. Life-saving. The setup was surreal. Customers walked through rows of roses to pick up our burgers. TikTokers filmed themselves navigating bouquets for delivery pickups. One tweet still makes me laugh: "Only in Tower Hamlets would you find Bengali brothers selling burgers from the back of a flower shop." But here's what happened behind those flowers: We stripped everything to the bone. No dining room overheads. No server wages. Just us, a £100 grill, and laser focus on the perfect burger. Whilst other restaurants fought to save their dining rooms, we mastered what people actually wanted: delivery excellence. The "backwards" move taught us forward thinking. That flower shop partnership didn't just keep us alive. It made us London's highest-rated burger joint. Pride kills more businesses than competition ever will. I see entrepreneurs clinging to status symbols whilst their bank accounts drain. The fancy office. The prestigious location. The "way things should be done." Sometimes the most successful move looks like complete failure from the outside. Sometimes you have to bloom where you're planted, even if it's behind the roses. What would your business look like if you stripped away everything except what actually drives results?

I've been using AI wrong this whole time. For months, I tried getting it to create viral food photos for our burger joint. It gives me specific tips: adjust the shadows under the patty, boost the saturation on the lettuce, sharpen the bacon edges. My first result? A Wagyu Bacon Burger that looked like actual food porn instead of AI slop. But here's where it gets interesting. This "AI as coach" philosophy is now how we're starting to operate across everything. We feed our 2850+ Google reviews (4.9 stars) into AI systems that analyses patterns invisible to human eyes. Then it coaches our front-of-house team with surgical precision. Not replacing our people. Making them superhuman at reading customer needs. The insight that changed everything: AI isn't good at creating. It's incredible at teaching. It can't make a perfect burger photo, but it can teach you to see light and composition like a pro photographer. It can't serve customers, but it can turn your team into service ninjas by analysing thousands of data points you'd never notice. We're not just London's highest-rated burger joint anymore. We're staying there because we learned the difference between automation and elevation.

I was the only brown kid in my entire French town. At age 8, I cried when I heard we were moving to London. Last week, I went back to visit my childhood best friend for the first time in years. We grew up together in Dieppe, a small beach town in Northern France. His family was Turkish. Mine was Bengali. We were the only two non-white families in town. When I moved away, I thought I'd lost everything. Sitting in his kitchen last week, catching up over Turkish tea and nuts, something beautiful happened. My rusty French came flooding back. We talked about his upcoming wedding, how the town had changed, what we'd built in our separate lives. Years of distance just melted away. Here's what struck me most: That 8-year-old boy who cried about leaving didn't know he was about to learn the most valuable lesson of his life. When you're forced to find community again, you learn something crucial. Belonging isn't automatic. You have to work for it. Community isn't just there. You have to build it. Connection isn't passive. You have to reach for it. Growing up as the only brown family taught me to value community in a way I never would have otherwise. Moving to London and having to start over taught me that you get belonging by giving it first. It's why community is at the heart of everything I do with Simply Smashed now. Not because it's good for business. Because I know what it's like to not have it. The thing that scared me most at 8 became my greatest teacher.

A Domino's Pizza now sits where my family's restaurant empire began. 40 years ago in Dieppe, France - 120 miles away from Simply Smashed My father opened the only Indian restaurant in town. Locals crossed the street to avoid the unfamiliar smells drifting from his kitchen. But he wasn't building alone. My mother was there by his side. Grinding spices at 9 AM. Perfecting recipes until midnight. Creating magic in a kitchen the size of most people's closets. The business lived two completely different lives. Summer brought packed tables and tourist laughter. They'd count the day's takings and dream of expansion. Winter brought brutal reality. Empty dining rooms. Heating bills that swallowed their savings. Nights spent wondering if they'd make it to spring. Most people would have seen the seasonal struggle as a reason to quit. Dad saw it as education. Every challenge was inevitable when you're building something from nothing. The secret wasn't avoiding difficulty - it was accepting it as the price of progress. I built the highest rated burger joint in London. 4.9 stars, 3000+ reviews. Those two years taught me more about building than any MBA ever could. The thing about the food industry is nothing is theoretical. From day one you're making decisions with real money on razor thin margins. One bad weekend and you feel it in your bank account by Friday, not next quarter. → We got burgled → I dealt with literal fires → One supplier issue and the whole menu changes overnight → I had staff not show up while I was two hours away with no way to get back → You learn to read people very quickly because you genuinely don't have time not to Simply Smashed started from a kitchen we were already using and maybe £100 on a new grill. That was the entire business plan. When every pound counts you develop this instinct for what's worth spending on and what isn't. That instinct doesn't go away when you move into tech. It just gets applied differently. Every decision I make building Draper now, whether it's hiring, spending, prioritising, I can trace back to something I learned in that kitchen. That's not from a textbook, it's from a Friday night that went sideways. And honestly I'd take someone who's survived a Friday night service with half their staff missing over someone who's only ever seen pressure in a case study. It's the most expensive MBA that I never paid for tbh

We raised £26,000 for charity through an app where every like was worth 1p. We made exactly £0 in revenue. I was 18. First year of my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs. I met the co-founder in the basement prayer room. We'd just finished praying and I asked him how he was doing, just being polite, and he mistook it as me asking how the app was doing. This man was probably mid-thirties, been at Goldman for years, and he just started telling me about this social media platform where every like triggered a micro-donation to charity. I had no idea what he was talking about. But I was in. That's how MiniDeed started for me. 1p, 2p, 5p. Tiny amounts that added up across 25 countries over two years. We onboarded Islamic Relief, Human Relief Foundation, a bunch of smaller orgs. We got featured in The New Arab. And somehow built a community where people were opening up about mental health because the whole vibe was just different. Users told us it was the only app where they felt safe doing that. Honestly watching the live donation ticker go up was more addictive than any MRR dashboard I've looked at since (and I say that as someone who now stares at dashboards for a living). We never figured out how to make money from it. Donations still trickle through the app daily, years later. But it was my first real taste of building something and I think about it all the time. 18 years old, sitting in Goldman Sachs by day, shipping a charity app by night. It led me to build the highest-rated burger joint in London. And now Draper.

I once hired a Boris bike to deliver a missing chicken burger to a customer's front door. He grabbed the bag, and shut the door without a word. We were mid-rush at Simply Smashed, maybe a Friday night, orders stacking up on the UberEats tablet. I checked a bag going out and realised we'd missed an item. Chicken burger, already paid for, already on its way to someone's house minus the thing they actually wanted. So I called the customer. Got the address. It was like a 5 minute cycle away. I ran outside, tapped a Boris bike, put the bag in the basket and just started pedalling through Whitechapel. Got there, knocked on the door, slightly out of breath. The guy opens it, looks at the bag, takes it, and closes the door. No thank you, no eye contact, nothing. I stood there for a second like... cool. Then I cycled back to the shop and got on with service. The thing is, I'm not telling this story because the guy was rude. He probably didn't even clock what just happened. He ordered food, food arrived, life continued. That's honestly fair enough. I'm telling it because that's what the early days of building anything actually feel like. You sprint to solve a problem nobody asked you to sprint for. You over-deliver by a stupid amount. And the response is silence. The guy didn't leave a review. He definitely didn't sign up for a loyalty program. I'm fairly sure he didn't even realise the founder just personally cycled a chicken burger to his door. Just a closed door and a Boris bike to return. And you go back and do it again the next night because that's the job. The gap between what you put in and what you get back is enormous when you're starting out. You have to be okay with that gap or you won't survive it.

Content is product. Product is content. I've said it maybe 200 times now. Most founders nod and then go do the opposite anyway. We ran Simply Smashed with zero paid marketing. Literally zero. We were just documenting the messiness of building a burger joint from the back of a flower shop and posting it, and that was doing the job a £5k/month ad budget would've done. We became the highest-rated burger spot in London and never boosted a single post. Then MiniDeed happened. The product was good and the impact was real and nobody knew it existed. The thing about having no distribution is it doesn't matter how good your product is. Nobody sees it. Completely opposite outcomes that somehow taught me the exact same thing. The founders who get this are building content into the product from day one. The GTM isn't a department you bolt on in month six, it's the whole thing. If you just raised and you're trying to decide whether to invest in content or put it off, the thing you're actually deferring is distribution.

I built the highest rated burger joint in London. Last month I walked into one that made me take notes. I had a stopover in Sweden, hadn't slept, needed a meal. Searched for halal options and this place popped up. Highest rated burger joint in Gothenburg. Smash burgers. I couldn't not go. The owner was North African, Algerian I think. The food was properly good. But the thing I'm still thinking about weeks later isn't the burger. Next to the counter they had coffee and these homemade North African biscuits laid out. Free. Take as many as you want. You could tell someone had made them that morning. People remember experiences. The burger was great but it's the coffee and the biscuits I keep coming back to. It's never the main thing. It's the thing next to the main thing that nobody asked for.

Side project of the week: I built an AI that composes music and then removes the music from itself. vibenasheeds: the claude for making vocal nasheed beats. Some of you might remember the lofi Muslim YouTube channel I posted about last year. I was making nasheed beats after 12-hour shifts at Simply Smashed because I could not find halal background music. Every nasheed pack was either £30+ per beat or so rinsed that you'd hear the same track in three different Muslim creators' videos on the same day. That whole channel was a test run... I've been cooking this up quietly between everything else. vibenasheeds is the actual thing. You prompt the vibe you want for your scene and AI generates a full track from scratch. Then what I'm calling the halal engine kicks in and separates the stems and strips the instruments out of the file, gone. What's left is vocals and daf. It composes with instruments first because that's how you get something that actually sounds good, then removes them... sounds like a weird extra step but the output is better (and I spent an embarrassing amount of time looking). The thing about the nasheed scene right now is the creators in it are incredible. I grew up watching them figure out an entire genre from scratch with basically nothing. You ever watch Chris Howett cycling through the mountains of Switzerland on an electric scooter? Half of why that youtube content hits the way it does is the audio. Muslim creators have been locked out of that entire dimension, you're either using the same 50 beats as everyone else or you're working in silence and hoping the visuals carry it. I want to describe what I'm hearing in my head for a specific moment and have it exist. Link in comments to try it out!

I was building an AI company between burger orders and honestly I miss it. I keep looking at this photo and it's kinda crazy. Simply Smashed was on its second location. Peruvian Street Kitchen was on its first. And somewhere in between both of those I decided this was also where I'd start building an AI content company on Replit. I had my laptop wedged into whatever corner I could find, squinting at code I barely understood while delivery drivers walked in and out. I'd be mid-prompt and someone would shout that orders were backing up so I'd get stuck in packing rice boxes and saucing them up. Then come back to my laptop trying to remember what I was even building. If the rush got too much the laptop just got closed and that was that. I'd been training writers at a ghostwriting agency and I could see so clearly that the whole industry was about to flip. Like I could literally feel it. And I had this thing in my head going if I don't start building this right now, from this kitchen, on this dying laptop, someone else is going to do it and I'll be watching from behind a fryer. It wasn't a plan btw. I didn't sit down and map anything out. Two food brands running, a kitchen that's too small for any of this, and my brain just going "yeah but what if we also built a tech company from here." I physically couldn't not do it. That was a couple of months ago. Draper is now past ramen profitable and growing every month. Peruvian Street Kitchen is opening its second physical location soon iA. Everything is better now. Better setup, better tools, actual laptops that work. But I keep coming back to this photo because something about building from that kitchen felt different and I can't fully explain why. P.S: I'm a firm believer that being in the trenches means delaying your trim, you have to earn it as a reward.

England crashed out of the World Cup semis yesterday and somehow I was the happiest person in the room. You know that scene in Avengers where Red Skull says "I guide others to a treasure I cannot possess," that's basically been my experience owning a restaurant for two years. We built Simply Smashed to be this communal living room where people come to watch games and hang out, and I've watched hundreds of people have that exact experience but I've never actually had it myself because I'm always behind the counter or thinking about what's broken or what needs ordering. Yesterday Sifat was running everything so I could just... sit. I had a strawberry cheesecake milkshake and the aircon was on and the whole room was going through it together as England went out and it was genuinely one of my favourite days at the shop. I still heard an Uber order get cancelled from across the room and it set off alarm bells in my head so it's never going to be the same as walking in fresh. But it was close, and that was enough. P.S: Spain it's all on you now, this is Mikel Merino's World Cup 😉

I keep entering domains the slow way in the fastest era in history. Twice now and I'd do it again. You can go to Claude right now and start building in a domain you have zero expertise in. And it might work tbh, in fact, we're in the most competitive era of software in history because of that. So why would you go into a domain you haven't earned? Go into the one where you've put the most reps in. That's your edge now. We grew Simply Smashed to the highest rated burger in London organically and that whole experience pulled me into writing for founders at agencies. I did that for a year, which led to Draper. With Vibenasheeds same thing. Grew a YouTube channel first, figured out what hit and what didn't, then started building. It reminds me of something Abdel once said to me... AI gets you 60% of the way there, it's on you to fill the gap. That 60% is everything that's ever been publicly scraped. The other 40% doesn't exist in any dataset. You learn it in the arena. P.S: If you want a break from the arena Kotor (it's like a less busy lake como) is one of the most underrated places in Europe, definitely recommend :) .

The Peruvian Thigh sold out in 3 hours on Monday. Most founders would be celebrating. I'm spending my days restocking and my evenings doing something most people don't realise restaurants need to do. Restocked at 8pm yesterday. Down to 2 left today. I'm literally restocking again as I write this. While everyone's buzzing about the 9s and 10s out of 10 we're getting, I spent yesterday doing the thing I can't stop myself from doing. 4 hours on the floor. Talking to every single customer who ordered it. Not because anything's wrong - the feedback has been insane. People are losing their minds over how tender the chicken is. Sure, one or two people said it wasn't for them. That happens. But here's what nobody tells you about launching food products: The recipe is maybe 20% of the work. The other 80%? Building systems so your staff don't ruin it. This isn't home cooking. You can't just hand someone a recipe and expect magic. I'm spending the next 2 months training every cook on exact timing. Quality control checkpoints. How to handle the marinade. When the chicken is perfectly done vs. overdone. The real skill isn't making good food. It's cutting through the noise of feedback to find what actually matters. Every "this is perfect" gets weighed against every valid criticism. What are people actually saying? What do they mean? How do we take all this data and find the one thing that improves our product? Our first Simply Smashed burger? Complete disaster. Not because the recipe was bad, but because we had no systems. No training. No quality control. I'm not a chef. But I know how to learn. How to gather feedback. How to iterate. It's very easy to get lost in the "yay, we launched a burger" celebration. But that's not it. It's the obsessiveness. The continuous improvement. The gathering data. Making sure we've got the systems in place. It's not sexy work, but it has to be done. While competitors are already planning their next launch, I'm still perfecting Monday's systems. Excellence isn't just a recipe - it's a system that delivers it every single time.

I abandoned my restaurant mid-service to bike across London while my kitchen was on fire. "Just sell chicken burgers until I get back," I told my team. Then I ran out the door. The cables had just burst into flames. Smoke filling the kitchen. My dad took one look at the melting electrical panel and rattled off exactly what I needed from Screwfix. So there I was - racing through 20 London lanes on a Santander bike, while customers wondered why beef burgers suddenly went "out of stock." Someone spent £100 trying to sabotage my stealth launch. And honestly? It's hilarious. So we're quietly testing PSK (Peruvian Street Kitchen). Not advertising. Just fulfilling random orders. Day 1: This guy orders from Simply Smashed. We go all out - extra portions, made with love, the works. Check the app that night: 1 star. Day 2: SAME GUY orders from PSK. Wait. We're in stealth mode. How did he even find both brands? Whatever. We try even harder. Make it perfect. That night: Another 1 star. Then the smoking gun: Someone left a 1-star Google review. On our brand new listing. Two hours after I created it. We hadn't even taken a single order yet. That's when I knew. This wasn't about the food. After that, this guy starts trying to order from BOTH brands. Every. Single. Day. Since leaving those 1-star reviews, he's attempted nearly £100 worth of orders. We just keep rejecting them. The Uber Eats account manager was like "yeah you can just ban him" so casually. Like this happens all the time. Because it does. The food business is weirdly tribal. There's literally takeaway wars happening up north right now. Actual wars. Over chicken shops. When I first started Simply Smashed, this stuff destroyed me. I'd see a fake review and spiral. Question everything. Lose sleep wondering what I did wrong. Check the reviews obsessively. Let it consume my whole day. My confidence would shatter. I'd second-guess every decision. Now? I recognise the pattern immediately. Competitor sees you doing well. Competitor panics. Competitor attacks. It's actually validation. Someone is SO pressed about our quiet little test that they're burning their own money AND time stalking our Google listings. The shift happened when I realised: You can't control the tribal nonsense. You can only control the food you make and how you treat real customers. Their panic is just noise. Your focus is the signal. These days when I see this behaviour, I don't spiral. I smile. Because if someone's willing to spend £100 trying to stop you... You must be doing something right. Anyway, we're thinking of adding him to our loyalty programme. At this rate, he'll get a free meal by Tuesday.
