I've left Simply Smashed. After 2 years of building the highest rated burger joint in London, I'm stepping back. My brother's taking over day-to-day. I'm building something new. It's strange to write that. This was never supposed to be my thing. My dad has been in the food industry for over 35 years. Started in a tiny French seaside town called Dieppe where it felt like we were the only asian family around, been doing this since before I was born. The restaurant was always his world. Then my parents got on a flight to Bangladesh and lockdown got announced mid-air. Me and my brother suddenly had a restaurant with no customers, staff who needed paying, and rent that didn't care about pandemics. We ran the Help Our Heroes campaign, delivered thousands of pizza slices to hospitals across London, kept the lights on for months. When we started thinking about selling, a buyer came in and made my dad feel like a fool. Said we were "bleeding out." Made a lowball offer so insulting my dad slammed the table and walked out. They just smirked and lit cigarettes outside. That led to a chain of events which led up to starting Simply Smashed. We launched three concepts at once. Simply Smashed just happened to be the one that took off. A £100 grill. Tables pushed away. The front space rented to a flower shop so people walked through flowers to pick up their burgers. We had no money to do it properly so we just told people what we were building and let them watch us figure it out. Today we're rated 4.9 stars. The highest rated burger joint in London. Looking back now it's hard to separate Simply Smashed from my family. My dad showing up every single time we needed him. My brother building operations that actually worked. My sister-in-law who created half the recipes we still serve today. We got review bombed for stocking Salaam Cola and the community showed up for us. Grateful for all of it. This was always a family thing. It still is. My brother has been with us from early and I trust him completely to take Simply Smashed and Peruvian Street Kitchen forward. I'm not disappearing - I'll still be around for strategic oversight. But the day-to-day is his now. Excited to see where he takes them both. I'm building something new. Can't say much yet but if you followed the Simply Smashed journey, you know the playbook. More soon iA.

I've been using AI wrong this whole time. For months, I tried getting it to create viral food photos for our burger joint. It kept spitting out fake-looking garbage with weird textures and plastic-looking elements. Then I realised something that changed everything. Instead of asking AI to replace my work, I started using it as my editing coach. I upload my real burger photos to ChatGPT and say: "Help me make this pop." It gives me specific tips: adjust the shadows under the patty, boost the saturation on the lettuce, sharpen the bacon edges. My first result? A Wagyu Bacon Burger that looked like actual food porn instead of AI slop. But here's where it gets interesting. This "AI as coach" philosophy is now how we're starting to operate across everything. We feed our 2850+ Google reviews (4.9 stars) into AI systems that analyses patterns invisible to human eyes. Then it coaches our front-of-house team with surgical precision. Not replacing our people. Making them superhuman at reading customer needs. The insight that changed everything: AI isn't good at creating. It's incredible at teaching. It can't make a perfect burger photo, but it can teach you to see light and composition like a pro photographer. It can't serve customers, but it can turn your team into service ninjas by analysing thousands of data points you'd never notice. We're not just London's highest-rated burger joint anymore. We're staying there because we learned the difference between automation and elevation.

I've been lying to you. Every time you saw me at Simply Smashed, there was something I wasn't telling you. For the last two years while I was running the restaurant, I was also advising Series A founders on their content strategy. Part time, on the side, mostly in secret. I was on calls with YC founders and A16z portfolio companies, founders building companies that will be household names in five years. And I was taking those calls from my restaurant. There's this memory I keep coming back to. I'm on a call with a founder talking positioning, narrative strategy, how to become the voice of their space. Elite player. The kind of person you'd expect to be advising from some nice office somewhere. And I'm standing next to our Simply Smashed punching machine. I had to be on site that day. Couldn't leave. So I just found a corner, put my noise-cancelling headphones on, and took the call anyway. My resume said: Restaurant Owner. My calendar said: Strategy Call with a16z Portfolio Company. They had no idea where I was. Most people didn't know I was doing this at all. Here's how that even happened. When Simply Smashed took off, people started asking how we did it. Highest rated burger joint in London with no marketing budget. Pure organic storytelling. My brother saw it before I did. He introduced me to someone at a content strategy agency - the kind that works with YC founders and a16z portfolio companies. They were looking for someone. My brother knew this was exactly what I'd been doing without realising it. That someone was Mustafa Khan, ACA. Who would end up becoming my co-founder. I said yes immediately. Everything I'd learned at Simply Smashed was from first principles. Pure instinct. I wanted to see what this looked like at scale with the smartest founders in the world. That became my arena. I started advising founders. Got them over 25M+ views across X and LinkedIn Then I got promoted to Head of Training. Responsible for training writers and creative directors on how to do what I'd been doing on gut feel alone. And it fit like a glove. Looking back, the thread was always there. Every project I've ever worked on grew through storytelling. I just didn't have words for what I was doing. It was instinct compounding over years. Last year I left the agency with Mustafa. We're building Draper. AI agents plus human taste for founder storytelling. Same instinct that's been compounding this whole time. Same playbook that took a burger joint to number one. Now we're helping other founders do it for their companies. we've been cooking like crazy btw. can't wait to share more.

Let's address the elephant in the room - most AI content is garbage. Here’s why: LLMs copying from other LLM generated articles. Repurposed slop from Reddit dressed up as insights. You can feel it when you're scrolling. It all sounds the same. But here's what I've learned about content that actually works after working with YC and A16z founders. When Simply Smashed took off, it wasn't because we posted more than anyone else. It was because we told our story. In our voice. People could feel the difference. That's why they kept showing up. The founders I worked with who won - same thing. Their story, told properly, compounding over time. The thing is, most founders don't have time for this. They're building. You can't cook with one hand on a phone trying to document yourself. You need both hands in the work. That's what me and Mustafa kept talking about. Builders should be focused on building. AI should be documenting you cooking. That's what we're building with Draper. Right now the human taste is us. We work with founders closely to get their voice right. But we're codifying what we've learned into systems. The vision is the human taste becomes you. Your stories. Your voice. The way you actually talk. Not repurposed slop. But actual authentic human stories that's told at scale. Right now we're deep in LinkedIn. But the vision is bigger. Content engines for entire teams, not just founders. Content marketing is shifting on how companies attract customers, investors and talent (will share more on this soon). We're building the infrastructure to make it scalable. we've been heads down cooking too. finally got some time to pull out the phone. lots to come, more soon.

I built the highest rated burger joint in London. 4.9 stars, 3000+ reviews. Those two years taught me more about building than any MBA ever could. The thing about the food industry is nothing is theoretical. From day one you're making decisions with real money on razor thin margins. One bad weekend and you feel it in your bank account by Friday, not next quarter. → We got burgled → I dealt with literal fires → One supplier issue and the whole menu changes overnight → I had staff not show up while I was two hours away with no way to get back → You learn to read people very quickly because you genuinely don't have time not to Simply Smashed started from a kitchen we were already using and maybe £100 on a new grill. That was the entire business plan. When every pound counts you develop this instinct for what's worth spending on and what isn't. That instinct doesn't go away when you move into tech. It just gets applied differently. Every decision I make building Draper now, whether it's hiring, spending, prioritising, I can trace back to something I learned in that kitchen. That's not from a textbook, it's from a Friday night that went sideways. And honestly I'd take someone who's survived a Friday night service with half their staff missing over someone who's only ever seen pressure in a case study. It's the most expensive MBA that I never paid for tbh

We 2x'd our deep work without adding a single hour to the week. it's the best thing we've done for Draper and it cost us literally nothing. Mustafa brought this from his old agency. When he first suggested it I remember thinking it was a bit rigid but we tried it anyway and honestly it changed how we work completely. → Monday and Wednesday: all client calls, stacked back to back → Tuesday, Thursday, Friday: just building That's it. (revolutionary stuff I know) The thing is most founders think they have a time problem. They don't. They have a transition problem. That Gen Z meme where someone books two hours before a meeting to stress about it and one hour after to recover is funny because it's basically true. The actual work takes 15 minutes but the mental commute between tasks eats the rest of your day. A 15 minute task that felt impossible at 3pm just flows on a quiet Tuesday morning. So we stopped trying to manage it and just stacked everything. six months in and honestly I don't think we could go back.

We raised £26,000 for charity through an app where every like was worth 1p. We made exactly £0 in revenue. I was 18. First year of my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs. I met the co-founder in the basement prayer room. We'd just finished praying and I asked him how he was doing, just being polite, and he mistook it as me asking how the app was doing. This man was probably mid-thirties, been at Goldman for years, and he just started telling me about this social media platform where every like triggered a micro-donation to charity. I had no idea what he was talking about. But I was in. That's how MiniDeed started for me. 1p, 2p, 5p. Tiny amounts that added up across 25 countries over two years. We onboarded Islamic Relief, Human Relief Foundation, a bunch of smaller orgs. We got featured in The New Arab. And somehow built a community where people were opening up about mental health because the whole vibe was just different. Users told us it was the only app where they felt safe doing that. Honestly watching the live donation ticker go up was more addictive than any MRR dashboard I've looked at since (and I say that as someone who now stares at dashboards for a living). We never figured out how to make money from it. Donations still trickle through the app daily, years later. But it was my first real taste of building something and I think about it all the time. 18 years old, sitting in Goldman Sachs by day, shipping a charity app by night. It led me to build the highest-rated burger joint in London. And now Draper.

What happens when you post a real Monet and say it's AI? The coolest art social experiment I've seen in a while. Someone posted a painting online and told people it was AI-generated. Asked them what made it inferior to the original. "Looks like sh*t." "Not as vibrant as Monet's typical palette." "Achieving maybe 20% of the real thing." People went in. It was a real Monet. The actual painting. And honestly the interesting thing here isn't the framing lesson everyone's pulling from this. It's what it tells you about where AI sentiment is right now. People looked at a masterpiece and called it garbage because someone told them a machine made it. They weren't evaluating the painting at all. The word "AI" just did all the work before their eyes even caught up. We run an AI native agency. The founders we work with are producing stuff that's good. Really good. But I know that if you slapped "AI-generated" on some of these posts, the same people who are engaging with them right now would suddenly call it slop. Same post, same words. You just changed what people think wrote it. One of the founders we work with said something about this that stuck with me. If a human writes something mediocre, people think everyone has an off day. If AI writes something mediocre, people think zero effort. That's the Monet experiment in one sentence. I don't think the gap between what AI can actually do and what people think it can do is closing anytime soon.

Content is product. Product is content. I've said it maybe 200 times now. Most founders nod and then go do the opposite anyway. We ran Simply Smashed with zero paid marketing. Literally zero. We were just documenting the messiness of building a burger joint from the back of a flower shop and posting it, and that was doing the job a £5k/month ad budget would've done. We became the highest-rated burger spot in London and never boosted a single post. Then MiniDeed happened. The product was good and the impact was real and nobody knew it existed. The thing about having no distribution is it doesn't matter how good your product is. Nobody sees it. Completely opposite outcomes that somehow taught me the exact same thing. The founders who get this are building content into the product from day one. The GTM isn't a department you bolt on in month six, it's the whole thing. If you just raised and you're trying to decide whether to invest in content or put it off, the thing you're actually deferring is distribution.

The founders with the most interesting things to say are the ones who never have time to post. Everyone knows volume matters. That's not controversial. Most founders fail at content because they're not posting enough and they know it. AI has made the volume problem basically solvable. You can generate a post about anything in seconds. But volume without quality is just noise. And quality is the bit that's actually hard to scale because it comes from somewhere specific. It comes from context. The thing you said on a call when you were explaining your vision to a new hire. A rant about why your industry does something backwards. The moment on a podcast where the cogs start turning and you forget anyone's listening. That's what we've been building at Draper. We call it excavation. We plug into the places founders are already being brilliant and mine for the stuff that's actually worth posting. Their calls, their meetings, the moments where they go deep and the real thinking comes out. AI collapses everything around that. The editing, the structuring, all the manual stuff that used to make content a full time job. (we're an AI content startup saying this btw, take from that what you will) But as producing content gets easier, the thing that's actually going to be competitive is the angles. The excavation. The stuff that already lives in the best founders' heads. We just need to figure out how to get it out of you. That's the problem we're trying to solve honestly. We're still cracking it but it's getting sharper every week.

I got 6 A*s and 5 As at GCSE. Then I got BBDD at A-level. Nobody's mentioned the GCSEs since. But I still hear about the A-levels. At 16 I was coasting and I didn't even know it. I thought being smart was a personality trait and not something you actually had to maintain. And A-levels are the moment the system stops rewarding you for being quick and starts asking if you can actually sit down and do the work. I could not sit down and do the work. BBDD hit and everyone knew. That's the thing about public failure when you've been publicly impressive, people do the maths for you. But I think about it now and that was the first time I learned anything useful. Everything I've built since, the restaurant, the agency career, Draper, came from a version of me that got humbled at 17 and finally figured out that showing up when it's boring is the entire game. Fear of God's Essentials hoodie retails at £180. I built one that beat their fabric specs for £60. It sold out in 3 hours. The product isn't why it sold out though. The storytelling is. So here's how that even happened. I went to Bangladesh and spent time studying how the supply chains behind brands like Fear of God actually work on the ground. I started building SIMPLYCLO from there. Our hoodie came in at 364 GSM, Fear of God's Essentials sits at 347. We were using the same factories in the same country with better fabric weight at a third of the price. None of that honestly matters if nobody knows you exist. So I documented the whole thing. I posted the factory visits, the fabric sourcing, ran brand name polls on Twitter, made TikToks from Bangladesh showing the entire process. Every single decision was made in public. Someone in Selfridges recognised the hoodie on me five weeks after we conceived the brand and said they'd already heard of it. We hadn't spent anything on ads or PR, it was all just content. It sold out in 3 hours. People had watched the whole story unfold in real time and by the time the hoodie dropped they felt like they were part of it. That's what actually moved units, not the GSM. SIMPLYCLO was a passion project and honestly one of the most fun things I've ever built. I ended up closing it down, but the thesis stuck with me. Content was the entire go-to-market. I just documented the build and let people in instead of spending anything on ads or PR.

Side project of the week: I built an AI that composes music and then removes the music from itself. vibenasheeds: the claude for making vocal nasheed beats. Some of you might remember the lofi Muslim YouTube channel I posted about last year. I was making nasheed beats after 12-hour shifts at Simply Smashed because I could not find halal background music. Every nasheed pack was either £30+ per beat or so rinsed that you'd hear the same track in three different Muslim creators' videos on the same day. That whole channel was a test run... I've been cooking this up quietly between everything else. vibenasheeds is the actual thing. You prompt the vibe you want for your scene and AI generates a full track from scratch. Then what I'm calling the halal engine kicks in and separates the stems and strips the instruments out of the file, gone. What's left is vocals and daf. It composes with instruments first because that's how you get something that actually sounds good, then removes them... sounds like a weird extra step but the output is better (and I spent an embarrassing amount of time looking). The thing about the nasheed scene right now is the creators in it are incredible. I grew up watching them figure out an entire genre from scratch with basically nothing. You ever watch Chris Howett cycling through the mountains of Switzerland on an electric scooter? Half of why that youtube content hits the way it does is the audio. Muslim creators have been locked out of that entire dimension, you're either using the same 50 beats as everyone else or you're working in silence and hoping the visuals carry it. I want to describe what I'm hearing in my head for a specific moment and have it exist. Link in comments to try it out!

One of my closest friends got married in the Spanish mountains a couple weeks ago. I came home and built an AI because of it. The ambience was unreal. He had a playlist that was perfect for the mountains. It felt so elegant and classy, perfectly suiting the event. And I kept thinking about how hard it is to get that feeling when you're trying to keep it halal. Vibenasheeds.com is this small hobby side project I've been building that composes music and then strips the instruments out of itself so you're left with pure vocals and daf. Every track runs through a halal verification gate, a neural net scoring across 527 sound classes looking for anything that shouldn't be there. I put it out there and within a week: - 110 minutes of original beats generated - 65,000+ instrument checks run - 6 times the AI tried to sneak an instrument in, caught every one I've had signups from content agencies, startups, a Muslim crowdfunding platform, creators from the UK, Denmark, the Netherlands. People I've never met making halal nasheeds because a wedding in Spain hit me a certain way. I'll cherish that one for a long time.

I keep entering domains the slow way in the fastest era in history. Twice now and I'd do it again. You can go to Claude right now and start building in a domain you have zero expertise in. And it might work tbh, in fact, we're in the most competitive era of software in history because of that. So why would you go into a domain you haven't earned? Go into the one where you've put the most reps in. That's your edge now. We grew Simply Smashed to the highest rated burger in London organically and that whole experience pulled me into writing for founders at agencies. I did that for a year, which led to Draper. With Vibenasheeds same thing. Grew a YouTube channel first, figured out what hit and what didn't, then started building. It reminds me of something Abdel once said to me... AI gets you 60% of the way there, it's on you to fill the gap. That 60% is everything that's ever been publicly scraped. The other 40% doesn't exist in any dataset. You learn it in the arena. P.S: If you want a break from the arena Kotor (it's like a less busy lake como) is one of the most underrated places in Europe, definitely recommend :) .

lofi.text: Every Muslim creator faces the same impossible choice. Use mainstream beats that compromise your values, or create content in silence. I felt this firsthand running Simply Smashed. We had a strict no-music policy, but how do you create engaging content without sound? How do you build atmosphere in your restaurant when customers walk in? I tried everything. Different beats, different ambient sounds. Nothing quite fit the vibe I wanted. Eventually we settled on live sports in the background - it worked for the restaurant atmosphere. But the content problem remained unsolved. That's when I remembered my old fascination with vocal beats. What started as casual interest became urgent necessity. So I taught myself. Every single night after brutal restaurant shifts, I'd come home exhausted and spend 1-2 hours learning to craft beats. My fingers fumbling through software I barely understood. My ears slowly training to hear what worked. Seven weeks in, something clicked. My YouTube channel "Lofi Muslim" hit 130 subscribers. I'm averaging 300 views daily. Comments started flooding in from Saudi Arabia, France from creators across continents saying "Finally, something that fits." Then came the moment that changed everything. A complete stranger bought my first beat. I stared at that notification for minutes. Someone I'd never met just paid for something I created in my bedroom after a restaurant shift. That's when I realised this wasn't just solving my problem. Muslim creators everywhere are starving for options. They're compromising their values because quality alternatives barely exist. Now I've got beats on Spotify and Apple Music. Creators are using my work in their content without me doing any marketing. The beat store is growing. But here's what really gets me: In an era where we consume endlessly, building something people actually want feels revolutionary. Lmk what you think! Do you vibe with the beats? Side project of the week: I built an AI that composes music and then removes the music from itself. vibenasheeds: the claude for making vocal nasheed beats. Some of you might remember the lofi Muslim YouTube channel I posted about last year. I was making nasheed beats after 12-hour shifts at Simply Smashed because I could not find halal background music. Every nasheed pack was either £30+ per beat or so rinsed that you'd hear the same track in three different Muslim creators' videos on the same day. That whole channel was a test run... I've been cooking this up quietly between everything else. vibenasheeds is the actual thing. You prompt the vibe you want for your scene and AI generates a full track from scratch. Then what I'm calling the halal engine kicks in and separates the stems and strips the instruments out of the file, gone. What's left is vocals and daf. It composes with instruments first because that's how you get something that actually sounds good, then removes them... sounds like a weird extra step but the output is better (and I spent an embarrassing amount of time looking). The thing about the nasheed scene right now is the creators in it are incredible. I grew up watching them figure out an entire genre from scratch with basically nothing. You ever watch Chris Howett cycling through the mountains of Switzerland on an electric scooter? Half of why that youtube content hits the way it does is the audio. Muslim creators have been locked out of that entire dimension, you're either using the same 50 beats as everyone else or you're working in silence and hoping the visuals carry it. I want to describe what I'm hearing in my head for a specific moment and have it exist. Link in comments to try it out!

We gamified Quran memorization with burgers and milkshakes. Here's why 100+ huffadh are loving it: Walking through East London Mosque, you see them everywhere. Brothers in corners perfecting every ayah of the Quran. Some staying up late, others coming at Fajr. Many of us struggle to just finish reading the Quran during Ramadan. But these huffadh (memorizers) perfect it completely - verse by verse, chapter by chapter. And they do this every single year. Most don't realize the sacrifice: • Months away from family • Time off work • Countless hours of revision • Mental strain of perfection That's why we launched our "Road to Ramadan" campaign at Simply Smashed. We've gamified their Quran revision journey: • 5 chapters = Punch on our machine • 10 chapters = Milkshake • 15 chapters = Tiramisu • 20 chapters = Wings • 25 chapters = Loaded fries • Complete Quran = Everything + burger We're partnering with Europe's largest gathering of huffadh - where hundreds come to revise. When we started Simply Smashed, people said "just focus on the burgers." But it was never just about the food. We're about recognizing the people in our community who don't get enough recognition. The ones who sacrifice silently. The ones who serve others without praise. That's what barakah-based building means to us. Not maximizing profits. Maximizing impact. Sometimes that means Sisters' Nights. Sometimes Fajr Knights. And sometimes it means supporting those who preserve the words of Allah. It might not be much, but it's our way of saying: We see your dedication. We appreciate your sacrifice. ↓ This Ramadan, let's show our huffadh they're valued. Drop by Simply Smashed to support their journey and maybe catch them taking a well-deserved break between revisions.

These teenage brothers just recited the entire Quran from memory in 9 hours - finishing just 2 seconds apart. Here's why their story matters to our entire community: At dawn, Abdurrahman (15) and Saabiq (16) began their extraordinary challenge. Hour after hour, verse after verse, they raced through 6,236 verses purely from memory. By 4:30pm, they had achieved what takes most people years to accomplish. Their father walked through our doors, eyes gleaming with joy, his sons' achievement radiating through his proud smile. We've partnered with Quran Revision Project - Europe's largest gathering of Huffadh - for our Road to Ramadan campaign, offering free meals to these dedicated memorizers of the Quran. But this isn't just about food. It's about recognition. It's about saying: "We see you." Our Huffadh represent something profound in our community: The preservation of our heritage. The bridge between generations. The future of our spiritual leadership. Yet too often, these young champions go unrecognized: • Years of dawn-to-dusk dedication • Sacrificing typical teenage experiences • Balancing intense memorization with school • Carrying the weight of religious responsibility at such a young age This Ramadan, they'll lead Taraweeh prayers at their local mosque in Barking. Think about that - at 15 and 16, they'll guide hundreds in prayer. At Simply Smashed, we believe business isn't just about transactions. It's about strengthening the fabric of our community. It's about creating spaces where achievements like these are celebrated. Where young people feel seen, valued, and supported. Because when we uplift our youth, we elevate our entire community. When we celebrate their dedication, we inspire the next generation. When we show them we're proud, we give them the strength to continue. ↓ This Ramadan, let's commit to appreciating our Huffadh more. They're not just memorizing text - they're preserving our heritage, one verse at a time. Share this to show our young Huffadh: Your community stands with you. We see you. And we are incredibly proud.

When me and my brother moved to London we were really excited by the London Halal Food scene here in comparison to what we experienced in Dièppe.

I ended up eating out regularly to eat from everything this wonderful city had to offer.

Usually served with authentic crispy french fries sometimes stuffed inside and/or served separately.

It was happiness on a plate for me

A Grec Sandwich is a tender pitta bread sandwich that’s lined inside with a variety of North African inspired sauces and stuffed full with gyro meats that’s been roasted on a spit and then topped off with various oozing french cheese 🧀

I used to love the car journeys to Paris that I took to visit my uncle as child.

Paris is where most Muslims lived and where the Paris Halal food scene used to be buzzing. 

What me and my brother really looked forward to in those journeys was eating a Grec Sandwich.

I didn’t plan to build Simply Smashed – we built it to survive. In early 2020, just as the lockdown was being announced, my parents boarded a flight back to Bangladesh, leaving my brother, Sifat Ahmed, and me to manage our family’s Italian restaurant in East London. What was meant to be a routine trip turned into a months-long ordeal. Suddenly, we were on our own, struggling to keep the business afloat without knowing when our parents could return. Those months were some of the most intense and challenging of my life. Between finishing my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs, navigating repatriation flights to bring my parents, and even dealing with a burglary at the restaurant, it felt like we were up against a storm. We knew we had to go back to basics. We transformed the delivery experience, launched two critical campaigns, and even got featured on Islam Channel for our efforts to donate pizzas to NHS staff during the pandemic – all while operating from the red. This is why community is one of the foundations of our brand. Simply Smashed was born out of sheer necessity. It wasn’t a start from scratch; it was a start from survival. Today, we're proud to be a family-run business as the highest rated burger joint in London (4.9* 1800+ Google reviews) with a story grounded in resilience and community. Loved speaking to Areeb Siddiqui on his podcast about our journey and what's to come next!

Last night I saw the future of the UK Muslim startup scene. As part of team Deen Developers and a batch member in their buildathon, I’m proud to witness and contribute to what we’re building. We’re at such an exciting time in the UK Muslim tech scene, and it’s incredible to watch this community grow from infancy. Seeing founders with both talent and integrity working to make a difference is what makes this movement truly unique. Yes, there’s talk about how far behind we are compared to places like SF, but today showed just how optimistic we can be about bridging that gap. One of the founders did the opening recitation, setting the tone. We saw projects ranging from Quran and seerah apps to sadaqah platforms—all built with a deep grounding in faith. And by the way, I’m working on something special too, a project called Bilal—but that’s a story for another post. I’m grateful to be part of this moment and to support as many Muslim startups as possible. Let’s keep building, keep growing, and keep giving back, insha’Allah. Shout out to the incredible team at DD Ibrahim Javed Muntasir Syed Taz Latif Ibraheem R. just to name a few! Shout out to our roasters who came to support as always as they have since the beginning Shahzad Younas Ibrahim Khan Humayra Hanif And shout out to the batch members, that we’ve seen grow and develop throughout the programme Kaazim Zia Sadiq Dorasat Hamada Mahdi Dilwoar Hussain There’s so many more deserving of shoutouts apologies for missing people, they know who they are. Everyone really came together to make this possible. The future is bright inshaAllah.

Ever had 20 litres of white sauce spill all over your car? It happened to me. My mum had made a fresh batch of our signature white sauce—my brother Sifat Ahmed’s recipe inspired by his travels to New York and the halal carts there. I was transporting it to the restaurant when we realised the container wasn’t sealed properly. The sauce spilled everywhere. Twenty litres, gone. It felt like a disaster, but we couldn’t salvage the sauce—so we salvaged the situation. Right there, amidst the chaos, we started shooting content. We recorded the mess, the frustration, the absurdity of it all—and then we shared it. That content went viral. Hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok and Instagram. What started as a disaster turned into one of our most successful marketing moments. But the story doesn’t end there. One of my staff recommended his friend’s detailing business to clean up the car, and these boys did such an incredible job that I ended up hiring two of them for front-of-house at Simply Smashed. One of them, just last month, brought in over 100 five-star reviews by himself. When life gives you lemons, make marketing content. Setbacks have a way of leading to unexpected wins. Like the time we raised over £4,000 for charity after getting review-bombed—but that’s a story for another post. What setbacks have you turned into opportunities? Share your story—I’d love to hear it.

Three years ago, we borrowed a projector. This summer, we packed out a living room. When we opened Simply Smashed three years ago, it was during the Euros final. At the time, we were a dark kitchen, but we started getting requests to show the game. So, I borrowed a projector from a friend, put together some tables, and screened the final in-store. It felt like something was missing—a Muslim-friendly atmosphere to watch live sports. That night planted a seed. We weathered the storm as a dark kitchen, built our reputation, and became a Top Eats vendor on Uber Eats, a certification awarded to the platform's highest-performing restaurants. When we finally had enough together, we renovated the space with one clear goal: to create a communal living room. A Muslim-friendly "third space" where people could gather, relax, and feel at home. Fast forward to this summer, and we hosted our second Euros final. Alhamdulillah, we’ve come a long way. We’ve added two screens, brought in sofas, and designed the space ourselves to look and feel like a living room. The atmosphere was incredible, and the place was full. Our vision is to create a true third space for Muslims. If non-Muslims have pubs to see their regular community, why shouldn’t Muslims have something similar? An alcohol-free, music-free space where everyone, Muslim or not, can find their community outside the pub. It’s humbling to reflect on how far we’ve come, and it’s exciting to think about what’s next. Who knows where we’ll be by the next Euros, inshaAllah?

We ban men from eating at our restaurant. Well, on Sisters’ Nights, at least. At Simply Smashed, our Sisters’ Nights are one-of-a-kind: exclusive evenings where only women are allowed to eat in-store. These nights are about more than just food. They create a safe, welcoming space for women to relax, connect, and enjoy themselves. Our most recent Sisters’ Night was a collaboration with Shabbir Hassan’s Faith Space, where we hosted a Palestinian-themed evening. Faith Space brought in Palestinian speakers to share their stories, and 50% of the night’s proceeds were donated to Human Aid & Advocacy’s Gaza Appeal. Initiatives like these tie directly into the larger mission of Simply Smashed: elevating the standards of Muslim entrepreneurship. Why do we do things like Sisters’ Nights? Because the best way to inspire change isn’t by telling others what to do—it’s by leading with action. Since launching Sisters’ Nights, we’ve already seen other restaurants follow the trend and host their own versions. And that’s the goal. To show that initiatives like these are not only meaningful but commercially viable. And if they’re commercially viable, you’ll see other businesses follow—something we know all too well in the Muslim food industry. This is part of our wider approach of building with barakah and injecting creativity to inspire others. It’s about setting trends that strengthen our communities and create lasting change. If you’ve been to one of our Sisters’ Nights, we’d love to hear your thoughts. And if not—keep an eye out for the next one. PS: What do you think of the banner? Can anyone guess which brand I got inspiration from for the copy? (Hint: It’s from a chocolate.)

If you’ve got bad breath, we’ll give you a discount. Okay, not quite—but if you’re fasting on Mondays and Thursdays, you can claim 30% off during Maghrib time as part of our Winter Arc Campaign, which launched today at Simply Smashed. The idea behind this campaign actually started when I was 20. Back then, I ran a small campaign to encourage winter fasting. I designed a simple poster with a friend, left it in Islamic society prayer rooms alongside boxes of dates, and shared it online. Before I knew it, others were replicating it in their own spaces. That experience taught me something profound: small, intentional acts can inspire meaningful change. Fast forward six years, and we’re building on that same idea—this time through Simply Smashed. The Winter Arc Campaign isn’t just about discounts. It’s about encouraging good. It’s about making fasting feel accessible and inspiring, especially for younger Muslims. The early response has been incredible. Within hours, the campaign hit 1.2k likes on TikTok. People are sharing how Simply Smashed encourages them to reconnect with their values. To make it even more impactful, we partnered with the imam of East London Mosque & London Muslim Centre who shared a heartfelt reminder on the virtues of fasting. At Simply Smashed, we rarely offer discounts. When we do, it’s always tied to a clear purpose. Campaigns like this reflect our mission: to build with barakah, inspire others, and serve our communities in ways that align with our faith. If this campaign inspires even one person to fast, that’s a success. If it inspires others to create similar initiatives in their own spaces, that’s barakah. Let’s encourage more barakah based building.

Last night, we went from London’s highest-rated to possibly the UK’s highest-rated burger joint. 6 months ago, we became London’s highest-rated burger joint, sitting at 4.8⭐️ with 1,000 reviews. But milestones aren’t where you stop. They’re where you push harder. As of last night, we’ve reached 4.9⭐️ with 2,000 reviews—a milestone that reflects so much more than just numbers. This is about a vision my team and I hold dearly: to uplift standards, to inspire ourselves and others, and to show what happens when you strive for ihsan (excellence) every single day. We’ve always believed that the best time to double down is when you’re already winning. That’s the heart of barakah-based building—creating with intention, delivering with excellence, and ensuring every step we take is meaningful and impactful. I’m deeply grateful for everyone who’s been part of this journey. Every review, every kind word, and every bit of love you’ve shown has helped us reach this point. You’ve made it clear that Simply Smashed is more than just a burger joint—it’s a space built on community, values, and striving to be the best. Oh, and about that sticker on our window proudly proclaiming “Number 1 in London with 1,000+ reviews”? Maybe it’s time we update it. After all, going from number 1 to staying number 1 is worth celebrating. And we’re just getting started, inshaAllah. Let’s keep raising the bar together.

For many young Muslims, the Christmas season can feel isolating. The celebrations around them can make it seem like there’s nothing for them to take part in—like their Muslim identity holds them back. I want to change that. At Simply Smashed we’ve always said that whatever happens outside our doors—whether people feel uncomfortable, insecure, or confused about their Muslim identity—inside Simply Smashed, that identity isn’t just tolerated. It’s celebrated. That’s the heart of our Fajr Nights campaign. Here’s how it works: During the holiday period, kids who attend 10 consecutive Fajr prayers at their local masjid and get their attendance cards stamped by their imam will earn a free meal at Simply Smashed. It’s about more than the meal. It’s about helping kids build the habit of Fajr, yes—but it’s also about giving them a sense of pride and belonging. We want young Muslims to know that our tradition has its own beauty, that our community is something to celebrate, and that there is something for them during this season. The masjid is where they’ll feel that sense of community. And Simply Smashed is where we’ll reward and celebrate their efforts. Being Muslim doesn’t mean missing out. It means embracing something even greater. What are your thoughts on creating spaces that celebrate identity and community?

We turned our burger joint into a classroom for young French Muslims. For the second year running, Simply Smashed has hosted French exchange students, with my brother, Sifat Ahmed, teaching them English during the day while they explore London in the evenings. But this is about more than just learning a language. Growing up in Dieppe, a small seaside town in France, we didn’t have many Muslims around us. Finding community was tough, and balancing our French and Muslim identities was even harder. Sifat has been volunteering with this French exchange group Oui Love Trips for years because we know how valuable it is to have spaces where you feel comfortable as a young Muslim. Simply Smashed has become that space. A place where these kids can not only learn but feel proud of who they are. It feels like coming full circle. This is what the communal living room was designed for. To create a space where being Muslim feels normal. Where young Muslims can feel seen, heard, and celebrated.

The scrolls are here. The Quest for Fajr Knights begins. A scroll delivered to young warriors, calling them to rise with the dawn. This isn’t just about a free meal. It’s about creating a legacy, shaping habits, and showing the next generation that their faith is something to celebrate. Here’s the mission: • Pray Fajr every day for 10 days during the holidays. • Get your attendance card stamped by your local Imam. • Complete the quest and earn your reward—a feast fit for champions. Last year, Fajr Knights was simply an idea. This year, it’s a movement. We’ve added scrolls to turn the challenge into an adventure, making kids feel like heroes on a quest—because that’s exactly what they are. For too long, young Muslims have felt like bystanders during the festive season. Fajr Knights reminds them that our traditions are worth celebrating. It brings them back to the masjid, to their community, and shows them that staying connected to faith is its own reward. This isn’t just what Simply Smashed does—it’s who we are. We’re here to build more than just burger joints. We’re here to build pride, joy, and community. The scrolls have found their knights. Will they rise to the challenge? The journey begins at Fajr.

This weekend, I’ve been building something I’ve dreamed about for years. Young Muslims face so much emotionally, especially during their teenage years. Some of us were lucky to have an "Ameen" in our lives. That person in the prayer room who gave the right advice at the right time. But many didn’t have that privilege. So I built Ameen, your Muslim companion. Ameen provides comfort, shares relevant duas, and offers lessons from the Seerah. It’s not about fatwas or rulings—it’s about support when it’s needed most. I spent the weekend rapidly prototyping and shipped an MVP (check comments). It’s simple, not perfect, but that’s the point. The goal is to iterate quickly, collect feedback, and build something that genuinely resonates with its users. This same product thinking is what built Simply Smashed into the UK’s highest-rated burger joint. From data-driven menu designs to understanding what our community values most, product thinking has always been central to what I do. Even though Simply Smashed keeps me busy, I’ve missed building products like this. It’s about identifying a problem, understanding the user, and delivering value fast. Also, I’ve also been expanding my design skills as a product manager. Ameen has been a great way to put that into practice and push myself creatively while solving meaningful problems. Accuracy will get better but check it out now in the comments, what do you think?

A child stood up and led a talk after Fajr this morning. At Darul Arqam, our partner mosque, the Fajr Knights programme is in full swing. Kids are waking up for Fajr, sharing naseeha (advice) with each other, and strengthening their bond as a community. One child even led a talk today—a moment that reflected the confidence and leadership we hope to nurture. Afterwards, they shared breakfast provided by the mosque, laughing and enjoying the sense of connection these mornings are creating. When I was younger, trips to restaurants were special because they were such rare occasions. It’s those types of memories that stick with you—moments of joy, community, and pride. That’s what we hope to create and leave behind for these kids. This is what Fajr Knights is all about—not just prayer, but fostering community, identity, and pride. Looking forward to hosting the winners at Simply Smashed soon. But honestly? The real victory is seeing what’s happening right now.

Last night I went from serving burgers to sitting in the House of Lords discussing Britain's AI future. Here's the brutal truth about our tech competitiveness: The gathering was electric - filled with British founders and innovators all asking the same question: How do we stop falling behind in the global AI race? The harsh reality? We're already behind. London has world-class talent, but we're losing them to the US for three key reasons: • UK tech wages can't compete • British investors are too risk-averse • We don't give enough chances to emerging talent The irony cuts deep: Alan Turing gave Britain an early lead in computing. Now we're playing catch-up. But there's hope. The room was filled with successful founders eager to give back: • Jamie Crummie (Too Good To Go) • Meagan Loyst (Gen Z VCs) • And dozens more ready to help The message was clear: We need immediate action on three fronts: • Better support for founders • More competitive compensation • Increased risk tolerance from investors This conversation in the House of Lords wasn't just talk. It was a wake-up call. Britain gave birth to modern computing. Now it's time to reclaim our place in tech innovation. The talent is here. The hunger is here. The potential is here. We just need to act. ↓ If you're building in UK tech or want to help shape its future, let's connect. The time for action is now.

The hidden cost of Muslim businesses chasing "white validation"... A disturbing pattern I've noticed in London's Muslim-owned restaurants: I recently spoke to a Muslim café owner who said "too many Muslims moving into the area is ruining business." Another Muslim Italian spot owner proudly poured wine while telling me "we only have high quality customers here." This isn't just about serving alcohol. It's about a colonial mindset that's still living rent-free in our community's heads. Success gets measured by how many white customers come through the door. Values get compromised for validation. Look at Brick Lane: • Muslim-owned restaurants all serving alcohol • Most struggling to stay afloat • None questioning why their barakah feels empty They change their names for acceptance. They change their values for profit. They change their whole identity for a pat on the back. Part of me understands - many did this to survive in a different era. But the real damage? Their children are watching. They're learning that success means shrinking yourself. Growing up thinking you need to be less Muslim to be more successful. That's exactly why I built Simply Smashed differently. I wanted to prove you can run a proper food spot, stay true to your values, and still win. No alcohol. No compromise. Just great food and real community. The result? We get everyone through our doors - Muslims, non-Muslims, families, young professionals. Why? Because when you're confident in who you are, people respect that. We don't need validation from serving wine. We get it from serving great food and staying true to our principles. The next generation needs to see this. Success doesn't mean becoming less of who you are. It means being exactly who Allah made you to be. If you're building a halal business, remember: Your principles are your competitive advantage, not your limitation.

The most dangerous thing you can do is put successful people on a pedestal. Here's why pedestals kill dreams, and what to do instead: I used to think successful people were built different. That they had some special DNA that made them capable of achieving incredible things. But after building multiple businesses, I've realized something profound: Pedestals create mental barriers that stop you from achieving your dreams. When you put someone on a pedestal, you subconsciously tell yourself their success is unreachable. You create an imaginary gap between you and them that doesn't exist. The truth? They're just regular people who: • Failed countless times • Learned from mistakes • Stayed consistent • Picked the right moments Here's another dangerous thing about pedestals: When we put people on them, they start believing they have all the answers. Just because someone built a successful tech company doesn't mean they know the secret to happiness. Just because someone's great at marketing doesn't mean they understand the meaning of life. Success in one area doesn't equal wisdom in all areas. The moment I stopped putting successful people on pedestals, everything changed. Their achievements suddenly felt within reach. My ambitions started feeling achievable. Instead of seeing them as distant role models, I started seeing them as future peers. And here's the crazy part - when you shift this mindset, they naturally become your peers. So here's what you should do instead: Turn those pedestals into ladders. Break down exactly what made them successful: • Study their specific traits • Analyze their decisions • Learn from their mistakes • Copy their winning moves Because here's the truth: Everyone is human. Everyone has flaws. And everything they've achieved is within your reach. The question is: Are you going to sit back and admire from a distance? Or are you ready to start climbing? ↓ If this resonated, follow me for more insights on building businesses and achieving your dreams. I share everything I learn from running Simply Smashed, London's highest-rated smash burger joint, and other ventures.

I turned down franchise requests from Dubai and Toronto yesterday. Here's why saying no to fast money might be the best business decision you make: I've watched too many Muslim-owned food brands expand rapidly, only to collapse spectacularly. Two years ago, I sat in a franchise pitch meeting that opened my eyes. The presenters were ex-bankers who claimed they'd "cracked" the burger game. 90% of their pitch wasn't about the food or brand - it was about investment protection schemes and rapid expansion plans. That should have been the first red flag. But for many in our community, especially those struggling to adapt to the changing hospitality landscape, it looked impressive. Polished ex-bankers. Protected investments. Rapid growth promises. That brand doesn't exist anymore. And here's the tragic part: The owners walked away with their franchise fees. But the franchisees? They're left picking up the pieces. This pattern keeps repeating: • Quick franchise sales • Minimal support • Failed locations • Lost life savings That's why at Simply Smashed, we're taking a different approach: We won't expand until we're 100% ready. We're not just building a burger brand. We're building a legacy that needs to match the quality of our product. We're focused on optimising everything before we even think about scaling. Sometimes the bravest business decision is saying "not yet" to opportunity. ↓ If you believe in building sustainably over scaling quickly, follow me for more insights on principled business growth.

We gamified Quran memorization with burgers and milkshakes. Here's why 100+ huffadh are loving it: Walking through East London Mosque, you see them everywhere. Brothers in corners perfecting every ayah of the Quran. Some staying up late, others coming at Fajr. Many of us struggle to just finish reading the Quran during Ramadan. But these huffadh (memorizers) perfect it completely - verse by verse, chapter by chapter. And they do this every single year. Most don't realize the sacrifice: • Months away from family • Time off work • Countless hours of revision • Mental strain of perfection That's why we launched our "Road to Ramadan" campaign at Simply Smashed. We've gamified their Quran revision journey: • 5 chapters = Punch on our machine • 10 chapters = Milkshake • 15 chapters = Tiramisu • 20 chapters = Wings • 25 chapters = Loaded fries • Complete Quran = Everything + burger We're partnering with Europe's largest gathering of huffadh - where hundreds come to revise. When we started Simply Smashed, people said "just focus on the burgers." But it was never just about the food. We're about recognizing the people in our community who don't get enough recognition. The ones who sacrifice silently. The ones who serve others without praise. That's what barakah-based building means to us. Not maximizing profits. Maximizing impact. Sometimes that means Sisters' Nights. Sometimes Fajr Knights. And sometimes it means supporting those who preserve the words of Allah. It might not be much, but it's our way of saying: We see your dedication. We appreciate your sacrifice. ↓ This Ramadan, let's show our huffadh they're valued. Drop by Simply Smashed to support their journey and maybe catch them taking a well-deserved break between revisions.

These teenage brothers just recited the entire Quran from memory in 9 hours - finishing just 2 seconds apart. Here's why their story matters to our entire community: At dawn, Abdurrahman (15) and Saabiq (16) began their extraordinary challenge. Hour after hour, verse after verse, they raced through 6,236 verses purely from memory. By 4:30pm, they had achieved what takes most people years to accomplish. Their father walked through our doors, eyes gleaming with joy, his sons' achievement radiating through his proud smile. We've partnered with Quran Revision Project - Europe's largest gathering of Huffadh - for our Road to Ramadan campaign, offering free meals to these dedicated memorizers of the Quran. But this isn't just about food. It's about recognition. It's about saying: "We see you." Our Huffadh represent something profound in our community: The preservation of our heritage. The bridge between generations. The future of our spiritual leadership. Yet too often, these young champions go unrecognized: • Years of dawn-to-dusk dedication • Sacrificing typical teenage experiences • Balancing intense memorization with school • Carrying the weight of religious responsibility at such a young age This Ramadan, they'll lead Taraweeh prayers at their local mosque in Barking. Think about that - at 15 and 16, they'll guide hundreds in prayer. At Simply Smashed, we believe business isn't just about transactions. It's about strengthening the fabric of our community. It's about creating spaces where achievements like these are celebrated. Where young people feel seen, valued, and supported. Because when we uplift our youth, we elevate our entire community. When we celebrate their dedication, we inspire the next generation. But I felt an unusual sense of peace. When you've rebuilt from zero before, you learn what truly matters: • Reviews don't build great businesses - processes do • External validation is temporary - excellence is permanent • Numbers can disappear - quality never does At Simply Smashed, we've built a culture of ihsan (excellence). I hobbled across a busy London road with 3 stacked burgers, wearing a protective boot. The journey from photoshoot to London's highest-rated burger joint taught me 5 crucial lessons: When we started, we couldn't afford professional photography. So there I was, against doctor's orders, in a protective boot, balancing burgers in traffic. But that's what it takes. Here's what I learned: 1. Start with what you have Don't wait for perfect conditions. We used an iPhone, natural light, and pure determination. Your resourcefulness matters more than your resources. 2. Pain is temporary, regret is forever My foot needed rest, but my dream needed action. Sometimes you have to push through temporary discomfort for long-term success. 3. Documentation is crucial Those early photos? They became our first marketing materials. Every struggle is content. Every setback is a story. Document your journey. 4. Consistency compounds We showed up every single day. Even when sales were low. Even when we were exhausted. Even when it felt pointless. The result? We became London's highest-rated burger joint in just 12 months. 5. Your 'why' must be bigger than your excuses We weren't just building a restaurant. We were creating a space where quality meets community, where halal food meets innovation. The most important lesson? There are no days off when you're building something you're truly passionate about. But passion alone isn't enough - it's the daily grind, the unsexy work, the showing up when nobody's watching that makes the difference. ↓ If you're in London and want to taste what happens when passion meets persistence, visit us at Simply Smashed.

Why we're closing our restaurant for the first week of Ramadan... And why it'll cost us 30% of our monthly revenue: Most restaurants are rushing to capitalize on Iftar sales right now. So we give them this time to: • Reset mentally • Connect with family • Focus on their spiritual journey But we don't stop there. Throughout Ramadan, we only open an hour before Iftar. This is our open prayer policy. But our vision goes beyond us. Imagine a network of accessible prayer spaces across the UK—cafés, restaurants, and businesses creating solutions for the community. This is our step forward, and we hope it inspires others to join us. We build with barakah, and we're proud to serve our community in more ways than one. How we built London's highest-rated burger joint with 8,500+ five-star reviews using product development principles instead of culinary training. Our secret? Obsession with data-driven iteration. From my product management background, I applied rapid testing methodology to burger creation. Our first burgers were terrible. We started by giving them to friends and family with one instruction: "Don't hold back." After incorporating their feedback, we moved to real customers, sharing our journey openly on social media. Six months in, with costs mounting and improvements seeming marginal, we almost abandoned the approach. But we persisted, collecting data on every aspect of the burger experience for 18 months straight. We didn't guess what customers wanted - we measured it. What seemed like small details made massive differences: • Testing different bun-to-patty thickness ratios for the perfect bite • Discovering that two pickles created better balance than three • Finding the perfect sauce-to-patty ratio through dozens of variations Our data revealed something surprising: customers preferred fewer, more perfected options. So we eliminated customization and whittled down from dozens of combinations to just three signature burgers. Each of these three burgers represents hundreds of iterations, refined by thousands of data points. The reviews started pouring in: • 2,500+ Google reviews • 6,000+ Uber Eats reviews • Highest-rated burger joint status in London (possibly UK) When our Uber Eats reviews were completely wiped due to a platform issue, I wasn't worried. Within just three months, we regained "Top Eats" status - their highest merchant rating. That's when I knew our system worked perfectly. What makes our approach different: • Family-owned with family-developed recipes • Product development mindset applied to food • Every decision backed by customer data • Systems that could rebuild reputation quickly when needed This approach didn't just create better burgers - it built a resilient business. Our customer loyalty grew with each iteration as we earned their trust through consistent quality. Now, I'm looking to expand our delivery radius across London and eventually the UK. I'm seeking commercial partners with established delivery networks who are equally ambitious and can match our vision for the next 2-3 years. We have the systems in place now - we need partners who can support our growth while maintaining our obsessive quality standards. If you're a delivery platform interested in bringing London's highest-rated burgers to more customers, let's connect. The lesson extends beyond food: When you obsessively iterate based on real customer data and build systems that can withstand challenges, you create products people can't stop talking about.

So he got my mum obsessing in our home kitchen 12 years ago, before Simply Smashed even existed. Her perfectionism created London's first halal tiramisu. Then COVID hit our Italian restaurant. Dining died overnight. Revenue vanished. Staff went home. But we had something special: a 12-year-old innovation that filled a gap others ignored. We launched tiramisu delivery across London - full trays of 24 slices for families and celebrations. The "tiramisu response unit" drove 40% of our revenue during the hardest months. That pivot saved us. After COVID, we opened Simply Smashed, and this dessert became our signature - the perfect finish after a hearty meal. The traits I inherited from my family: • My mom's obsession with perfection (months of testing until it's exactly right) • My brother's ability to spot cultural market gaps (seeing what others miss) • The belief that real innovation starts in the home kitchen, not a boardroom That same process is happening right now. A couple days ago for Eid, my mom was back in the same home kitchen, months into perfecting our new pistachio tiramisu. Testing different pistachio ratios, adjusting the cream texture, making sure every layer brings that same joy our original recipe has delivered for over a decade. She's treating this new flavor with the same obsessive care that saved our business during COVID. The same kitchen. The same perfectionism. The same family innovation process that created London's first halal tiramisu. This week, we're finally ready to share that joy with everyone else. We're launching pistachio tiramisu at Simply Smashed - another family creation moving from our home to your table. Sometimes the smallest innovations create the biggest moments of joy. The landlord had one requirement: sell beer. We said no and left. A while back, I was standing inside this perfect empty pub thinking about everything we could build there. 18 months it had been sitting vacant. Dust on the windows, chairs stacked on tables, that sad emptiness of a place where people used to gather. But I could see it transformed: families sharing smash burgers where bar stools used to be, kids laughing where drunk arguments once happened, our punching machine where kegs used to sit - people competing to beat the high score instead of drowning their sorrows. The space was perfect. The rent was reasonable. The location had everything we needed. Then the landlord restrictions hit us like a cold slap. Heineken owns the building. Every tenant must sell beer on the premises. No exceptions. For our halal concept, that's not just impossible - it goes against everything we stand for. I felt that familiar knot in my stomach. The same one I get when people suggest we "just add a few non-halal options" to capture more customers. This wasn't about finding a loophole. This was about a company stuck in 1995 trying to force 2025 businesses into their dying model. Here's what most people don't understand: since 2000, the UK has lost 15,800 pubs. That's 35% of them completely gone. Last year alone, 490 more closed permanently. This isn't random bad luck. This is what happens when you build your entire business model around something people increasingly don't want. Meanwhile, we're building spaces where everyone belongs. Where great food brings people together instead of alcohol dividing them. Where a Muslim family and their non-Muslim neighbors can share the same table without anyone feeling excluded. That empty pub sitting there for 18 months? Perfect metaphor for what happens when you refuse to evolve. I walked out feeling disappointed for exactly two hours. Then I realized something: Heineken's inflexibility just saved us from partnering with a company that fundamentally doesn't understand the future we're building. We're not just opening restaurants. We're proving that the old model of social spaces - built around exclusion, centered on alcohol, designed for a narrow demographic - is finished. Every time an established player tells us our approach won't work, the market proves them wrong. Every time someone says we're being too restrictive by staying halal, our customers show us the opposite: they're hungry for spaces that don't require them to compromise their values. The same family obsession with perfection that saved us during COVID. That perfect location is still out there somewhere. When we find it, the landlord will understand what we're building instead of trying to force us into their expired playbook. Sometimes the best opportunities come disguised as closed doors. This one just reminded us why we're building something completely different.

Charity has become too easy. And that's the problem. We've turned giving into a finger tap, losing what it means to help. Here's why we need to bring back physical giving: Everything's been abstracted away. Tap to donate. Swipe to give. Click to help. This convenience comes at a cost that goes deeper than we realize. Research suggests that physical acts of giving may activate different reward pathways in our brains compared to digital donations. When we physically hand over our contribution, we get psychological feedback that a simple tap can't replicate. But it's not just individual psychology. Physical giving rebuilds social fabric. This aligns with what we believe at Simply Smashed - that giving rebuilds community. That's why we're partnering with HumanAid on this Syria relief campaign. Instead of digital donations, we set up a physical drop-off point where people bring food, toiletries, clothes, and nappies. I started this just a couple days ago and the container is already nearly full. The community has really showed up. I've watched a ripple effect happen in real-time. One person brings donations, their neighbor sees them loading the car and stops to ask about it. The psychological shift is visible. People arrive planning to drop off one bag, then see the community response and return later with more. Digital giving requires one decision. Physical giving requires dozens - what to bring, when to go, how much to carry. Commitment psychology research shows that each choice deepens investment in the outcome. This doesn't mean digital giving is worthless. For people with disabilities, busy schedules, or limited resources, online donations are often the only viable option. But for those who can choose, there's something irreplaceable about showing up. These containers go directly to those in need, but the real value is bringing people together around shared purpose. We have until 27th June as a drop-off point, so just 3 more days left. If you're in the area and want to contribute, there's still time. Physical giving creates stories. Digital giving creates receipts. Next time you want to help, consider showing up instead of just paying up. Find a local drive, volunteer at a food bank, or organize something in your neighborhood. Your presence matters as much as your money.

The Peruvian Thigh sold out in 3 hours on Monday. Most founders would be celebrating. I'm spending my days restocking and my evenings doing something most people don't realise restaurants need to do. Restocked at 8pm yesterday. Down to 2 left today. I'm literally restocking again as I write this. While everyone's buzzing about the 9s and 10s out of 10 we're getting, I spent yesterday doing the thing I can't stop myself from doing. 4 hours on the floor. Talking to every single customer who ordered it. Not because anything's wrong - the feedback has been insane. People are losing their minds over how tender the chicken is. Sure, one or two people said it wasn't for them. That happens. But here's what nobody tells you about launching food products: The recipe is maybe 20% of the work. The other 80%? Building systems so your staff don't ruin it. This isn't home cooking. You can't just hand someone a recipe and expect magic. I'm spending the next 2 months training every cook on exact timing. Quality control checkpoints. How to handle the marinade. When the chicken is perfectly done vs. overdone. The real skill isn't making good food. It's cutting through the noise of feedback to find what actually matters. Every "this is perfect" gets weighed against every valid criticism. What are people actually saying? What do they mean? We sold burgers from the back of a flower shop. And it saved our restaurant. Our full-service Italian restaurant was dying after COVID hit. My brother had what seemed like the worst idea ever: "Let's share space with a flower shop and focus on delivery only." I thought he'd lost his mind. Our runway was coming to an end. But when you're drowning, you grab any lifeline. He found the perfect partner - a flower shop that donated profits to Pakistani hospitals. Value-aligned. Rent-splitting. Life-saving. The setup was surreal. Customers walked through rows of roses to pick up our burgers. TikTokers filmed themselves navigating bouquets for delivery pickups. One tweet still makes me laugh: "Only in Tower Hamlets would you find Bengali brothers selling burgers from the back of a flower shop." But here's what happened behind those flowers: We stripped everything to the bone. No dining room overheads. No server wages. Just us, a £100 grill, and laser focus on the perfect burger. Whilst other restaurants fought to save their dining rooms, we mastered what people actually wanted: delivery excellence. The "backwards" move taught us forward thinking. That flower shop partnership didn't just keep us alive. It made us London's highest-rated burger joint. Pride kills more businesses than competition ever will. I see entrepreneurs clinging to status symbols whilst their bank accounts drain. The fancy office. The prestigious location. The "way things should be done." Sometimes the most successful move looks like complete failure from the outside. Sometimes you have to bloom where you're planted, even if it's behind the roses. What would your business look like if you stripped away everything except what actually drives results?

When Simply Smashed launched, we followed the playbook: "Give customers options." Pick your sauce. Choose your toppings. Build your perfect burger. The result? People just don't like their own choices sometimes. So we flipped the script. Instead of asking what customers wanted, we watched what they actually ordered. Which sauce combos got 5-star reviews? What toppings made people reorder the next day? Which "custom" creations never got built twice? After analysing thousands of orders, the patterns were undeniable. 3 combinations absolutely dominated everything else. So we killed the customisation chaos. No more endless menus. No more decision fatigue. No more mediocre experiments. Just 3 perfect burgers distilled from real customer behaviour. Our wagyu bacon? That's literally the #1 combination customers built when given total freedom. Each burger represents months of data, not gut feelings or chef ego. 18 months later: 4.9 stars, 2500+ reviews, #1 in London. Turns out customers don't want infinite choice. They want someone who's analysed infinite choice and picked the winners. The best service isn't more options. It's saying "Trust us. We've done the work.

I stole a water bottle and lost a BlackRock internship. I need to explain this properly because this is a pretty funny story. We were on a law firm insight day in sixth form and some kids decided to nick one of those fancy glass water bottles on the way out. And they were doing it so badly. Like embarrassingly badly. I basically went just give it to me and took over the whole operation myself. I was seventeen and it was a nice water bottle tbh I don't know what else to tell you. Now my head teacher was an ex-lawyer. So he didn't just tell us off like a normal person. He launched a full investigation. Students pulled in one by one. "But Sakib said you took it." By the end of it everyone hated everyone. I respect it looking back honestly the man missed his calling at MI5. I got internally excluded for two weeks. Fair enough tbh I did help steal a water bottle. They called me water bottle Sakib for the rest of sixth form. But then he went and called BlackRock. Personally. An internship I'd earned on my own and he killed it over a water bottle. His reasoning was I needed to "learn to appreciate the opportunities that come." So I went and applied through SEO Scholars entirely on my own. I didn't tell the school, didn't ask for a reference. Did the whole thing on my own. Got placed at a private equity firm where I didn't know a single person. That internship is what led me to Goldman Sachs. One of the youngest on their degree apprenticeship, first cohort they ever ran. Turns out he was right. I did need to learn to appreciate opportunity. And the best way was to find my own. The thing is years later Goldman Sachs did a profile on me. My head teacher shared it proudly. I wanted to thank him but to this day he still has me blocked on Twitter.
